stories.headline: Taiwan shuts down ahead of weakening Typhoon Champi, hundreds of flights cancelled
stories.deck: The administration ​said the typhoon’s radius was around 320 km (200 miles), large enough to ⁠cover most of Taiwan, and weather experts said its impact could last nearly two ‌days.
stories.bodyText:
Almost all of Taiwan shut down on Friday (October 23, 2026) ahead of the arrival of Typhoon Champi, which is forecast to bring strong winds and torrential rain, though the storm is weakening and is not expected to make direct landfall on the island.
At one point a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of around 191 kph (119 mph) near its centre, according to Taiwan's Central Weather Administration (CWA).
The storm was about 330 km (205 miles) east of Taiwan's southern tip, the CWA said. The storm's forecast track shows it will pass just off northeastern Taiwan, turn north toward the Chinese coast and eventually move into southern Japan.
The administration said its radius was around 320 km (200 miles), large enough to cover most of Taiwan, and weather experts said its impact could last nearly two days.
Taiwan's financial markets will also close for Friday (October 23), while only the Taiwan-controlled Kinmen islands, which sit next to the Chinese coast, will open schools and offices as normal.
The Transport Ministry said all 262 domestic flights were cancelled for Friday (October 23), along with more than 350 international ones.
Taiwan is generally very well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike in autumn, bringing strong winds and torrential rain.
The typhoon is forecast to first pass over Japan's westernmost inhabited island, Yonaguni, in Okinawa Prefecture.

stories.headline: Rice prices hit more than one-year high on strong rupee, tight supply
stories.bodyText: Indian rice export prices rose further this week to their highest level in more than a year, supported by a stronger rupee and modest demand amid tight supplies. India's 5 per cent broken parboiled variety was quoted at $387-$392 per ton this week, up from last week's $384-$389. Indian 5 per cent broken white rice was priced at $389 to $394 per ton. .Paddy hoarding, price rise force Karnataka rice mills to halt operations. The rupee has appreciated steadily over the past few days, prompting traders to raise export prices to reflect the exchange-rate movement, said a Kolkata-based exporter. The country's rice production is set to fall this year for the first time in a decade, and by the most in nearly 20 years, as below-normal rainfall during the crop's maturation period threatens to cut yields, industry officials told Reuters. Vietnam's 5 per cent broken rice was offered at $440-$450 per metric ton on Thursday, flat from a week ago. External demand remains stable, and we expect more orders from the Philippines coming in from mid-November, a trader based in Ho Chi Minh City said. Vietnam exported 228,871 tons of rice in the first half of October, raising its total shipments this year to October 15 to 6.6 million tons valued at $3.2 billion, according to the government's customs data. In Thailand, 5 per cent broken rice was quoted at $480 per ton, unchanged from last week, traders said. "Demand (is) coming from the Philippines. There are also vessels arriving to load rice, which has pushed prices up slightly," a trader said. "Supply is currently being harvested in some areas, so we need to wait and see the impact on production once the floodwaters recede," the trader added. .Government lifts curb on non-basmati white rice exports, removes floor price. Rice prices in Bangladesh remained elevated amid rising fuel costs, while aromatic rice prices surged despite the government's decision to cut approved export quotas by 50 per cent. The price hikes have added to the financial burden on consumers already struggling with persistently high inflation.

stories.headline: Judge orders Trump to give deposition in BBC lawsuit by December 11
stories.deck: Judge Enjolique Lett in Miami gave the order in response to complaints by the British broadcaster that Mr. Trump has refused to sit for a deposition, including canceling a previously agreed date of October 16
stories.bodyText:
A U.S. judge on Thursday (October 22, 2026) issued President Donald Trump a December 11 deadline to testify under oath in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC.
Judge Enjolique Lett in Miami gave the order in response to complaints by the British broadcaster that Mr. Trump has refused to sit for a deposition, including canceling a previously agreed date of October 16.
If Mr. Trump fails to attend the deposition by then, he risks sanctions, including dismissal of his lawsuit, the court said.
Mr. Trump has accused the BBC of deceptively editing its documentary "Trump: A Second Chance" to make it seem as if he was inciting violence when he told supporters to march on the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021, after losing the presidential election.
The crowd proceeded to storm Congress in an attempt to stop the formal certification of Democrat Joe Biden's victory.
While the BBC has apologised for the incident, which prompted the resignation of multiple senior executives, the broadcaster has denied it caused Mr. Trump any real injury and moved for the case to be dismissed.
Mr. Trump filed his suit against the BBC in December 2025 and is seeking at least $5 billion on each of two counts.
Charles Tobin, a lawyer for the BBC, said in court that Mr. Trump had no real excuse not to testify and that on October 16, he had only been campaigning, "participating in party politics."
"No plaintiff is above the law," Mr. Tobin said.
In a court filing Wednesday (October 21), Mr. Trump's legal team argued that he was not seeking to avoid a deposition but had been constrained by "matters of national importance."
The lawyers said Mr. Trump would be able to give a deposition between January 11 and 22.
Mr. Trump has made attacks on the media a signature of his two presidential terms, insulting reporters who ask questions he doesn't like and seeking to ban outlets airing critical reports from the White House.
Most recently, the administration has plunged into a legal dispute with CNN, MSNOW and Politico over attempts to bar them from the White House.
With his approval ratings in the low 30% range and polls showing his Republican Party likely to lose control of the House of Representatives in the November 3 midterm elections, Mr. Trump faces increasing headwinds as he approaches his final years in power.

stories.headline: Microsoft develops AI tool that can diagnose 'sequentially' like a doctor
stories.bodyText: Microsoft researchers say an AI tool that diagnoses patients step by step, as doctors do, was more than twice as accurate as general physicians at solving complex medical cases, according to a study published on Thursday in Science. The model identifies and coordinates the questions that should be asked of a patient, as well as the exams and tests that should be ordered, using an "orchestrator" that organizes how AI will tackle a problem by employing a simulated panel of clinical experts collaborating to solve diagnostic cases, according to the report. .Gadgets Weekly: Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra, ThinkBook 14x and more. Existing medical AI models typically take an all-at-once approach that examines all of a patient's symptoms, lab results and imaging studies to generate a diagnosis. With the orchestrator coordinating the steps to reaching a diagnosis, the AI model first decides what to ask about the patient’s history and what is significant in the physical exam. Based on what it learns, it decides which tests to order, considers the results, and orders further testing as appropriate. All the while, it is updating its working hypotheses and plans, the research leaders said in an interview. Tasked with diagnosing more than 300 highly unusual and confusing medical dilemmas, the model employing the diagnostic orchestrator was more than twice as accurate at "working up" the patient and determining the diagnosis as general physicians using textbooks and the internet. The tool also outperformed human physicians when presented with scenarios drawn from a major database of emergency room admissions. Assessments comparing these types of older systems to human doctors usually use multiple-choice questions, the researchers said. "AI has become very good at getting a 100% pass rate on those,” said Dr. Dominic King, the corporate vice president of the health unit at Microsoft AI, whose team is developing the new technology. “But of course, that's not real-world. No patient ever came to see me with a nice summary.” .TCS, Microsoft say PERM suspension will have limited impact; hiring strategy remains local-focused. The researchers also found that diagnostic processes cost less when the orchestrator designs the work-ups than when human doctors do. “We're not just measuring the accuracy of the systems. We're also measuring how judiciously and carefully it goes through a diagnostic work-up,” said Harsha Nori, head of AI at Microsoft AI Health. In a collaboration with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, the researchers will next test the tool’s ability to triage patients in emergency department waiting rooms.

stories.headline: Anahat scripts history, storms into maiden PSA Gold semi-final
stories.deck: Anahat Singh pulled off an impressive comeback against Salma Hany, clinching her spot in the semi-finals at a PSA Gold-level event after a nail-biting five-game match that lasted 42 minutes. The 18-year-old, facing a 1-2 deficit, demonstrated resilience and skill. Anahat will now go head-to-head with Malaysia's Sivasangari Subramaniam, reigniting their rivalry from the Asian Games final…
stories.bodyText:
Indian squash sensation Anahat Singh continued her giant-killing run at the Silicon Valley Open 2026, producing a remarkable comeback to defeat Egypt's Salma Hany in a five-game thriller and book her maiden semi-final berth at a PSA Gold-level event. The 18-year-old World No. 15 recovered from a 1-2 deficit to register a 4-11, 11-8, 4-11, 11-2, 11-5 victory over the sixth-seeded Egyptian in 42 minutes in Redwood City, California.
Anahat showed tremendous resilience after twice falling behind in the contest, raising her level in the final two games to complete an impressive turnaround. Having conceded the opening and third games, the Indian dominated the closing stages, dropping just seven points across the last two games to seal a landmark win.
The victory marks another significant milestone in Anahat's burgeoning career and comes on the back of her stunning second-round upset of eight-time world champion and World No. 3 Nour ElSherbini.
Anahat rallies from behind to seal historic victory
Hany made a strong start, capitalising on Anahat's errors to take the opening game 11-4. The Indian responded with an improved performance in the second, winning it 11-8 to restore parity.
However, the Egyptian regained control in the third game, cruising to another 11-4 win to move within a game of victory. 
With her quarter-final hopes hanging in the balance, Anahat produced a superb response, stepping up her intensity to dismantle Hany 11-2 in the fourth game.
The teenager carried that momentum into the decider, maintaining her composure and dictating the rallies to close out the contest 11-5. Her emphatic finish underlined her ability to respond under pressure against an experienced opponent.
The win ensures Anahat reaches the last four of a PSA Gold event for the first time in her career, further strengthening her growing reputation on the international squash circuit.
Asian Games final rematch awaits Anahat in semi-finals
Anahat's reward for the hard-fought quarter-final victory is a semi-final showdown against Malaysia's World No. 4 Sivasangari Subramaniam, who booked her place in the last four with a straight-games win over compatriot Rachel Arnold.
The clash will renew a rivalry established at the 2026 Asian Games, where Sivasangari defeated Anahat 3-0 in the women's singles final to claim gold, leaving the Indian with silver. Anahat had made history at the continental event by becoming the first Indian woman to reach the squash singles final.
Anahat has enjoyed an impressive campaign in Redwood City. She began by defeating Egypt's Nour Aboulmakarim 11-8, 11-8, 12-10 in the opening round before producing one of the biggest wins of her career against ElSherbini, beating the top-tier Egyptian 11-8, 11-8, 11-7.

briefs.headline: How India thwarted Pakistan’s bid to steal crucial defence data
briefs.deck: Officers of the Counter Intelligence Cell of Andhra Pradesh, intrigued by a slew of messaging patterns across various social media platforms, busted a major digital honey-trap racket, including the Indian conduits, whose motive was to leak sensitive defence details, specifically Naval intelligence, to the neighbouring country’s Inter-Services Intelligence, writes Sumit Bhattacharjee
briefs.bodyText:
About six months ago, a team of officers in Andhra Pradesh’s Counter Intelligence Cell (CIC) noticed an unusual pattern of messaging across various social media platforms, including interactive messaging applications such as WhatsApp.
What intrigued the officers was an abnormal frequency of incoming and outgoing international communications. The communication pattern was immediately red-flagged. The CIC team alerted central intelligence agencies and leveraged the resources of NATGRID (National Intelligence Grid) and CMS (Central Monitoring System) ֪— core components of India’s security infrastructure designed to combat terrorism, espionage, and cross-border threats — to trace Internet Protocol (IP) logs and WhatsApp One-Time Password (OTP) sharing patterns.
This initial anomaly marked the beginning of unearthing a far larger conspiracy and espionage racket involving the leaks of sensitive defence details — specifically naval intelligence — by Indian conduits to their handlers in Pakistan’s Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI).
After placing the subjects under close surveillance using a combination of technical intelligence (TechInt) and human intelligence (HumInt) for several months, a dedicated team of officers and personnel from Andhra Pradesh’s CIC, in close coordination with Naval Intelligence and Anti-Terrorist Squads (ATS) across 10 States, busted a major Pakistan-sponsored espionage network. The network reportedly focused on gathering field intelligence on the Indian Navy, with particular emphasis on the Eastern Naval Command (ENC).
Code-naming the crackdown as ‘Operation Firewall-2026’, law enforcement agencies moved in to execute arrests. In the process, investigators identified 18 key suspects, including 13 naval personnel spread across 10 States — Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Goa, Delhi, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Bihar, and Chhattisgarh.
The operation has so far led to the arrest of two individuals. Among them is Pradeep Mukherjee, a sailor in the Indian Navy posted at the ENC, who was taken into custody from INS Agrani in Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, where he was undergoing training. The second arrested individual is Annam Sai Varaprasad, a civilian contract driver engaged for naval officers at the Visakhapatnam naval base.
Although the coordinated operation was formally launched on October 1, the Andhra Pradesh CIC announced the arrests on October 5 and 6. The CIC stated that cases were registered under multiple provisions, including Section 61(2) (criminal conspiracy) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), Sections 17 and 18 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), 1967, Section 3 of the Official Secrets Act (OSA), 1923, along with other relevant sections of the BNS.
Mechanics of the espionage network
According to sources within Counter Intelligence, the operation followed a pattern typical of cross-border espionage. Pakistani Intelligence Operatives (PIOs) from the ISI identified vulnerabilities among potential targets, cultivating them to serve as assets within India.
The handlers deployed time-tested Vulnerability Mapping and the classic MICE (Money, Ideology, Coercion, and Extortion) framework to initiate contact, cultivate trust, and extract actionable information through digital honey-trapping combined with financial inducements.
“That is precisely why they consistently target sailors or lower-ranking personnel in the Navy — individuals who may be facing financial distress and need money,” noted a senior intelligence official.
In this instance, the operatives relied heavily on Social Engineering and open-source intelligence (OSINT) techniques. Handlers systematically scanned social media platforms to identify vulnerable defence personnel, government contractors, or civil servants before setting their traps.
According to a senior intelligence officer, digital honey-trapping served as the primary hook.
In such operations, fake female personas are engineered to initiate casual contact. Over time, these interactions graduate into romantic conversations, eventually leading to the exchange of sexually explicit content. While the investigation remains ongoing, preliminary findings confirm that explicit material was exchanged. However, investigators are still verifying whether these materials were subsequently used as leverage for blackmail to extract classified operational information.
Thus far, the investigation revealed that two trained female PIOs operating under the pseudonyms Joshita Pall and Anvi Mehta were in direct contact with the two arrested persons.
While Joshita claimed to be an employee at a shipbuilding firm in Mumbai, Anvi posed as a Delhi-based psychologist. The operatives initially established contact through Facebook before coaxing the targets to transition their conversations to WhatsApp.
Technical intelligence gathered by investigators indicates that the operatives approached defence personnel using fictitious social media profiles. Once rapport and trust were established, conversations rapidly shifted to text messaging, encrypted voice calls, and video calls. The broader strategy relied on fabricated professional identities, promises of romantic relationships, explicit adult content (including compromising video recordings), and monetary incentives paid via cryptocurrency channels.
According to a serving commander-rank officer, he had once received such unsolicited e-mail from a “very attractive-looking woman”, who posed as an executive in a communication company. But after a very mundane conversation, I could understand that it was a honey trap, as she sounded very keen to know about my rank, my postings and other confidential details. I broke the contact immediately. Later, I realised that she had picked up my profile from a matrimonial site, as at that time my parents and I were browsing through such sites. They look for vulnerabilities and target their needs and aspirations, he said.
A CIC official explained that initial conversations are typically mundane and centre on trivial matters. However, trained operatives gradually steer discussions toward sensitive operational domains, extracting fragments of information. They then connect these disparate data points to reconstruct operational theories or draft comprehensive intelligence briefs. In the current case, investigators allege that the ultimate objective was to persuade personnel to share classified defence intelligence.
The operatives reportedly sought intelligence regarding: movements and schedules of naval vessels and submarines. Photographs and video footage of naval assets and sensitive installations. The identities, routines, and movements of Commanding Officers. Live operational tours during video calls, where personnel were urged to show sensitive areas of naval bases, ships, and submarines.
It is now established that the names and profiles of these PIOs were completely fraudulent, with strong indicators suggesting they may have been generated using Artificial Intelligence (AI). It is a recognised reality in modern counter-espionage that foreign intelligence agencies, including Pakistan’s ISI, rely heavily on generative AI and deepfake technologies to conduct digital honey-trap operations.
The traditional “Romeo spy” methodology has evolved into AI-driven automation, primarily because synthetic profiles leave virtually no real-world human digital footprints for investigators to trace. Handlers use generative AI models to construct hyper-realistic human faces, photo galleries, and video clips that do not exist anywhere else on the open web, frequently leaving cyber-investigators without initial reference points.
Profile cloning, deepfakes, and real-time AI voice-swapping calibrated to match local accents are the latest weapons in the intelligence arena. Generative AI models can mimic regional dialects and cultural nuances, making conversations feel remarkably natural. Intelligence sources confirm that this specific technological dimension of the case remains under active investigation.
Why the focus remains on Vizag?
Pakistani intelligence has long maintained a focused interest in the Eastern Naval Command based in Visakhapatnam. Historically, during the 1971 Indo-Pakistani War, Pakistan deployed its most advanced submarine, the PNS Ghazi, to the waters off Visakhapatnam with the specific objective of tracking and sinking India’s aircraft carrier, INS Vikrant.
Visakhapatnam is not merely home to one of India’s largest naval bases; it serves as the home port for the Arihant-class nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines (SSBNs). These assets operate under the Strategic Forces Command (SFC) and represent a vital leg of India’s nuclear triad. Furthermore, the highly classified Ship Building Centre (SBC), where these nuclear submarines are constructed and fitted out, is located within this naval enclave.
Ever since India commissioned its first indigenous SSBN INS Arihant, foreign intelligence agencies have intensified efforts to gather granular details regarding the facility and its assets.
This operation is far from the first cross-border espionage case targeting the ENC.
In December 2019, Operation Dolphin’s Nose exposed an extensive spying network targeting the ENC. That investigation uncovered a network of Pakistani Intelligence Operatives who utilised digital honey-traps, hawala money channels, and local conduits to compromise junior naval personnel.
Initially detected and investigated by the Andhra Pradesh CIC, the 2019 case was subsequently handed over to the National Investigation Agency (NIA). Approximately 15 people, including seven naval personnel, were arrested, establishing direct links to the ISI. The NIA has since secured formal convictions against several of the key accused.
The operational methodology and the nature of intelligence sought in the current case bear striking similarities to the 2019 enterprise: detailed data on ship and submarine deployments, dockyard layouts, and base logistics.
In both instances, suspects were charged under stringent legislation, including the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), Section 3 of the Official Secrets Act (OSA), and Section 120B of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for criminal conspiracy.
In both cases, the primary objective of the PIOs was to obtain ground-level field intelligence regarding:
Operational deployments and departure schedules of surface ships and submarines. Official names, personnel files, and movements of Commanding Officers. Logistics, supply replenishment patterns, and base support protocols.
“There are various sophisticated avenues of intelligence gathering today, including high-resolution satellite imagery. Yet, field-level human intelligence remains one of the oldest and most reliable methods, and honey-trapping is the oldest trick in the operational handbook. It happened decades ago, and it will continue to occur,” observed a senior naval officer.
Every detail concerning a warship or submarine – no matter how minor – holds strategic value for an adversary. Photographs reveal structural contours, dimensions, radar cross-sections, and stealth modifications. Furthermore, acquiring advance knowledge of a naval vessel’s movement schedule makes it significantly easier for an adversary to pre-position intelligence-gathering ships or submarine-snooping units.
Such specialised units can collect critical operational signatures, including radar emissions, acoustic signatures, and electronic transmission patterns, enabling foreign militaries to fingerprint and track naval assets during conflict.
Even mundane administrative details such as, the exact volume of fuel, fresh water, and dry rations loaded onto a vessel prior to departure, provide vital clues regarding its intended operational range and sailing duration. This forms the core of tactical field intelligence, and the PIOs were tasked with systematically extracting these details from cultivated assets.
“PIOs engage targets in prolonged communications—alternating between casual banter and sexually explicit dialogue—to gradually harvest relevant data points and piece together a comprehensive operational picture,” the officer added.
Why field intelligence still matters?
Military history demonstrates that low-tech field intelligence has repeatedly neutralised or outmanoeuvred high-tech military capabilities.
During the 1971 Indo-Pakistani War, Indian Army field agents intercepted a logistics communication sent by the Pakistan Navy to local naval authorities in Chittagong (then East Pakistan). The message requested specialised diesel engine lubricants and heavy submarine-grade maintenance oils at Chittagong Port. This critical signal intelligence was corroborated by local Indian field intelligence agents and immediately passed to the Naval Intelligence.
By collating these reports, analysts confirmed the operational presence of Pakistan’s only long-range, U.S.-built diesel-electric submarine capable of extended operations in the Bay of Bengal – the PNS Ghazi. Intelligence analysts deduced that the Ghazi had been deployed specifically to locate and strike India’s aircraft carrier, INS Vikrant.
In response, Vice Admiral N. Krishnan, then Commander-in-Chief of the Eastern Naval Command, executed a classic deception operation. He ordered the INS Vikrant to sail to a secure, undisclosed anchorage near the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Concurrently, he intentionally leaked a false logistics requirement for massive ration procurements at Visakhapatnam, signalling to Pakistani intelligence that the Vikrant was still docked there.
Vice Admiral Krishnan arranged for a naval officer stationed aboard the Vikrant to send personal mail to his family from Visakhapatnam, ensuring the letters passed through local Pakistani intelligence channels.
The PNS Ghazi sailed directly into the strategic trap. The operation culminated in the destruction and sinking of the PNS Ghazi off the coast of Visakhapatnam on the intervening night of December 3-4, 1971, following targeted engagements by INS Rajput.
Similarly, decades later, intelligence monitoring revealed Pakistan’s bulk procurement of specialised extreme-cold-weather gear and high-altitude snow boots from European suppliers. This classic field-intelligence indicator exposed operational preparations prior to the 1984 Siachen conflict, allowing Indian forces to execute “Operation Meghdoot” and secure the strategic heights of the Siachen Glacier first.
The painstaking probe
Narrowing down the suspects in “Operation Firewall, 2026” required months of painstaking investigation. Once anomalous international messaging traffic was flagged, the AP CIC and central intelligence agencies deployed technical surveillance frameworks like NATGRID and CMS to intercept incoming and outgoing international communications, trace IP logs, monitor WhatsApp OTP sharing patterns, and isolate digital channels used to exfiltrate classified naval data. High-end decryption tools were used to decipher end-to-end encrypted messages.
Investigative sources confirmed that financial transactions and the real-world identities of the suspects were mapped using NATGRID databases. Money trails involving suspicious bank transfers, local hawala networks, and cryptocurrency micro-payments were traced across 10 Indian states.
A critical breakthrough occurred when investigators uncovered a local support architecture that utilised Indian SIM cards registered under fictitious or stolen local names. These local conduits shared One-Time Passwords (OTPs) with foreign handlers overseas. Indian intermediaries were enticed with monetary incentives—paid either in cryptocurrency or through local cash transfers—to supply the OTPs required to activate fresh WhatsApp accounts. Once activated, these messaging accounts were operated remotely from Pakistan by ISI handlers.
However, capturing digital footprints was insufficient to secure convictions.
“After conducting extensive digital surveillance, we immediately moved to gather simultaneous human intelligence (HumInt). It required months of synthesising both TechInt and HumInt before we possessed sufficient operational proof to execute the raids,” explained a CIC official.
A senior IPS officer involved in the operation detailed the complexity of counter-espionage investigations:
“Because this is an active national security investigation, full operational details cannot be disclosed. However, in cases of this magnitude, putting targets under surveillance and compiling actionable counter-intelligence takes months or even years. We utilise specialised methodologies, including launching proxy sites to entrap rogue actors.
While our technical capabilities operate within specific framework constraints compared to agencies in the US, Israel, or Russia, we routinely collaborate with partner nations to verify cross-border intelligence. The most challenging aspect remains retrieving encrypted message logs from foreign application developers and service providers, as they operate under strict user privacy contracts. Recovering data from platforms using end-to-end encryption requires demonstrating explicit national security threats to obtain high-level judicial and administrative authorisation, a process that can take weeks or months.”
Safeguards and Operational Security
In light of evolving cyber threats and cross-border espionage networks, the Ministry of Defence has instituted stringent operational security (OPSEC) frameworks across all service branches to safeguard classified assets.
Despite these protocols, the key question remains: How do foreign operatives continue to breach security perimeters, and how do compromised assets successfully transmit classified operational data?
The Armed Forces, including the Indian Navy, have banned a wide array of high-risk commercial applications and imposed strict regulations on Virtual Private Networks (VPNs). Personnel are explicitly prohibited from using social networking platforms, online gaming chat servers, or commercial VPN applications on both official and personal devices while stationed at sensitive bases or operational commands.
Despite these prohibitions, preliminary findings indicate that photographs and video recordings of sensitive military installations were successfully transmitted by the accused to their overseas handlers.
Military regulations mandate a strict “zero-tolerance” policy regarding unreported contact with unknown or suspicious foreign social media profiles. Service personnel undergo continuous training to identify and report suspected “honey-pot” solicitation attempts immediately.
Prompt reporting allows counter-intelligence units to initiate immediate “trap-and-trace” operations or feed coordinated disinformation back to foreign intelligence handlers.
While the CIC and collaborating intelligence agencies have conducted digital forensic audits on seized mobile phones, hard drives, and communication hardware confiscated from naval bases and private residences, officials have not yet disclosed the full extent of the classified material that was exfiltrated.
“We have initiated deep digital forensic recovery procedures to retrieve deleted chat histories, transmitted image files, and underlying metadata,” stated a CIC official.
Investigative agencies emphasise that the current arrests represent only the initial phase of a broader network breakdown. While 18 primary suspects have been formally identified and two individuals are currently in custody, additional arrests and detailed disclosures are anticipated in the coming days as forensic analysis proceeds.

briefs.headline: When mob takes law into its own hands: another man lynched in Keralam’s Palakkad
briefs.deck: The brutal lynching of an aurally challenged, unidentified man near the Moolathara dam in Keralam’s Palakkad has once again shaken the conscience of society. Abdul Latheef Naha speaks to investigators, psychiatrists and forensic experts to understand how did a homeless man become the target of a group that took it upon itself to punish him and such incidents are recurring.
briefs.bodyText:
The flesh looked pounded.
Contusions piled upon contusions. As forensic surgeon Hithesh Sanker examined the battered body that was laid on the post-mortem table, suspicion gave way to a grim realisation—this was no ordinary death.
The man had been lynched.
He had no name. He could not speak. He could communicate only through sign language.
Found dead near the Moolathara dam in Keralam’s Palakkad recently, the man in his late 30s bore nearly 50 injuries.
He was allegedly stoned and beaten with sticks for sleeping outside a house at Nedumpara.
Whatever he had tried to communicate, no one had understood or cared to.
By October 11, 2026 morning, the man, yet unidentified, lay dead. There was no known prior enmity or established offence.
The police registered an unnatural death. The post-mortem examination at the Government Medical College Hospital, Thrissur, revealed the brutality of the crime.
Similar incidents
The killing echoes two other brutal lynching in Keralam—of Madhu, a tribesperson beaten to death in Attappady in 2018 over allegations of stealing food, and of Ram Narayan Baghel, a migrant worker from Chhattisgarh lynched at Walayar in December 2025 on suspicion of theft.
The pattern goes back even further. In 2010, Rajendran, a 34-year-old man described as mentally unstable, was tied to a post and beaten through the night at Peruvemba. He died, and eight accused were sentenced to life imprisonment.
Different men, different circumstances, but a chilling common thread—the vulnerable become targets, suspicion becomes a verdict, and a mob assumes the power to punish.
Seven people were booked in connection with the killing. Kathiresan, one of the accused, is alleged to have led the attack. The victim had reportedly been sleeping in front of his house.
There were no apparent eyewitnesses.
Confession
The confession of one accused became a crucial lead, while investigators collected other evidence, including fingerprints. A 10-member special investigation team led by Chittur Deputy Superintendent of Police (Dy.SP) M. Sasidharan is pursuing the case.
“We have extended the search to different parts along the border. We have published the photo of the victim in various groups, including that of ASHAs, SC/ST promoters and local body ward members. We have informed different settlements along the border, both in Keralam and Tamil Nadu,” says Rajeesh S., Circle Inspector of Police, Kozhinjampara.
The search for his identity continues, but the killing raises a larger question: how did a homeless man become the target of a group that took it upon itself to punish him?
Recurring pattern
The Moolathara lynching reflects a recurring pattern—suspicion becomes accusation, and a crowd assumes the authority to deliver punishment.
P. Premnath, former Deputy Director of Prosecution, says India has witnessed numerous cases of mob lynching and cow vigilantism over the past decade. Earlier, prosecutors relied on provisions of the Indian Penal Code covering murder, rioting and unlawful assembly, including Section 149, which holds members of an unlawful assembly liable for offences committed in pursuit of its common object.
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), which came into force in July 2024, introduced Section 103(2), which provides for punishment for group murder on specified discriminatory grounds. “Its application depends on the circumstances of each case,” explains Premnath.
In its 2018 judgment in Tehseen S. Poonawalla vs Union of India, the Supreme Court laid down measures to prevent and punish lynching, including designated police officers, speedy trials and victim compensation.
Yet such violence persists.
“Responsibility should be established through evidence, and those found guilty should face the consequences,” says Premnath.
No suspicion or accusation gives a crowd the right to take the law into its own hands. “None has the right to hurt or take anyone’s life,” asserts Anees Ali, outgoing general secretary of the Indian Psychiatric Society’s Kerala unit. “There is no right to try anyone publicly.”
At Moolathara, the man may have been unwanted by those around him. He may have been unable to explain why he was there. Neither circumstance could justify violence.
Dayal Narayan, Head of the Department of Psychiatry at Government Medical College Hospital, Manjeri, says aggression is a human instinct, but civilisation depends on learning to control it. “Humans, like animals, have an instinct for aggression. It manifests in different ways, from road rage to violence on sports fields,” points out Dr. Narayan. Civilisation depends on learning to control these impulses, weigh consequences and resolve conflicts peacefully. But those restraints can fail, he notes.
“When people lose trust in social checks and balances, they take the law into their own hands. Some see it as heroism or an expression of solidarity; others believe they are serving a good cause. The aggressor becomes the hero,” he observes.
Once an assault begins, others may join in or reinforce the violence rather than challenge it. The group emboldens individuals, weakening their sense of personal responsibility. “Instead of correcting an action, group members tend to reinforce it,” notes Dr. Narayan.
Dr. Ali identifies personality, social conditioning and substance abuse as possible contributing factors. Alcohol impairs judgement and lowers inhibitions, while peer pressure and heightened emotions can further weaken restraint, he notes.
The prefrontal cortex, which governs judgement and impulse control, continues to mature into the mid-to-late twenties. But brain development alone cannot explain mob violence; social influences and individual choices also matter.
“Substance abuse is behind many crimes. Crimes due to substance abuse are increasing in the State,” Dr. Ali observes.
Dr. Narayan cautions against assuming that everyone involved in a group attack has the same psychological profile. Participation in a crime alone cannot establish a psychiatric diagnosis.
Mob psychology
The question is how ordinary social restraints fail so completely that a group stops recognising the humanity of the person before it. Forensic evidence often reveals violence that a community may not have witnessed or acknowledged.
P.B. Gujral, veteran forensic expert and former police surgeon who helped develop the Kerala Medico-Legal Code, says lynching can cause injuries more extensive than those seen in many other forms of homicide. “All murders are cruel and painful. But lynching is worse than any other form of murder,” he feels. Repeated blows from several people can cause extensive internal bleeding and damage to organs. Bruises accumulate, blood vessels rupture and injuries become fatal through their combined effect, say medical experts.
“They keep beating, piling injury upon injury,” Dr. Gujral says.
He recalls cases of group assaults in which victims suffered more than 100 injuries. The damage inflicted by a crowd can far exceed what any one participant might have caused alone.
“Even the weakest person who has not beaten someone in his life may take part in lynching. That is mob psychology,” Dr. Gujral says.
Dr. Sanker questions a society that fails to protect the vulnerable. “If literacy does not make us more humane, what purpose does it serve?” he wonders.
“A mob has no authority to administer punishment. Suspicion is not a crime, and an accusation is not a conviction,” he says. The victim’s inability to communicate or defend himself should have invited help, not violence. “Even though we do not know his name, we have a moral obligation to demand justice on his behalf.”
Proving the crime
Dr. Gujral notes that parts of Palakkad have witnessed repeated mass assaults in the past. Forensic evidence alone, however, cannot secure a conviction. “For a crime to be proven and convicted, it requires the cooperation of society,” he says.
Witnesses must speak, evidence should be preserved, and communities must resist pressure to protect those accused of violence. Fear and silence can weaken an investigation even when physical evidence is compelling, he feels.
Soumya P., a social worker from Chittur, calls the lynching a shame on the region. “Nobody knew such a brutal killing had taken place until the post-mortem revealed it,” she says. The attack, carried out at night in an isolated spot, went unseen by residents, she says.
People sleeping outdoors often remain outside the attention of families, neighbours and public services. Their isolation makes them harder to be protected.
Dr. Narayan says people should intervene sensibly when a confrontation threatens to escalate. Calling the police, seeking help and moving a vulnerable person to safety can prevent violence from becoming fatal.
“We need such people,” he says, referring to those willing to act when violence begins. Yet people too often walk away.
He also calls for sustained protection for people living on the streets, noting that efforts made during the COVID-19 lockdown should not disappear when an emergency ends.
Dr. Ali argues that awareness should reach young people and families. Dr. Narayan calls for cultural change beginning in childhood, when respect for others should be taught through everyday behaviour, not merely textbooks and slogans. Dr. Gujral stresses speedy trials and public awareness.
Though homeless and unable to make himself understood, the Moolathara lynching victim needed help, not hostility. His name remains unknown, yet his right to live was never in doubt.

briefs.headline: A greying population, a strained care system
briefs.deck: Gaps in geriatric healthcare and support systems leave many older people struggling to access medical care, find reliable caregivers, and cope with mental health concerns and social isolation. These challenges threaten their independence and quality of life, particularly among those from economically weaker backgrounds. With Telangana’s population aged 60 and above projected to grow over the next…
briefs.bodyText:
Girija (name changed) spent years working as a domestic worker before her failing knees made it difficult for her to continue. Hoping to find a more manageable way to earn a living, the 60-year-old borrowed money from acquaintances and set up a roadside vegetable stall. But another health problem emerged, making it difficult to keep the business running.
“She learnt that she was suffering from urinary incontinence. Taking frequent loo breaks while managing the stall was not practical, and she eventually decided to shut shop, losing her source of income in the process,” says Gurajada Sobha Pernidevi, founder-president of Telangana Stree Seva Samstha, a voluntary organisation working for the welfare of women.
For older people with limited financial means, a health problem can do more than cause physical discomfort; it can take away their livelihood, independence and opportunities to socialise. Conditions that are difficult to discuss, such as urinary incontinence, are often endured in silence because of embarrassment and the cost of managing them.
Unlike ailments that call for joint replacement surgery or a cardiac stent, these less visible difficulties of ageing often receive scant attention, despite their potential to disrupt daily life. However, as Telangana’s share of elderly population grows, addressing such overlooked needs will become increasingly important.
Telangana’s population aged 60 and above is projected to rise from 12.5% in 2026 to 17.1% in 2036, according to the Reserve Bank of India’s report, ‘State Finances — A Study of Budgets of 2025-26: Demographic Transition in India — Implications for State Finances’.
The State is expected to join the category of ageing ones, where senior citizens account for at least 15% of the population. The projected demographic shift raises questions about how healthcare, caregiving and community support can keep pace with the needs of older people, particularly those who live alone or cannot afford private services.
Associations working with senior citizens say the challenges range from obtaining medicines and reaching hospitals to finding dependable caregivers and accessing mental health support.
P. Shyam Kumar, State project coordinator at HelpAge India, says doorstep medical services, including palliative care, could make healthcare more accessible. Nutritional supplements and the delivery of medicines through Accredited Social Health Activists could also help older people manage their health.
“Without adequate support, their condition may deteriorate, leading to more hospital visits, additional expenses and greater dependence on family members. So, supplying medicines through Accredited Social Health Activists may work in this direction,” he adds.
The pace mismatch
Access to healthcare is not simply a matter of getting an appointment or obtaining medicines. Older people who depend on younger family members for hospital visits may have to wait until someone can take time off work and accompany them.
Members of several associations say a family member’s availability often influences whether and when an older person seeks medical attention. Those with limited mobility may need transport, a wheelchair or stretcher. In a multi-storey building without a suitable lift, even getting someone downstairs can require additional assistance and planning. Hospital visits can involve long walks between departments, diagnostic tests and consultations, making them particularly difficult for those without someone to accompany them.
The problem does not end at the hospital gate. For older people who cannot leave home, finding a doctor willing to make a home visit can be equally difficult. “This is a crucial requirement of those who are unable to step out of their house,” says Sobha.
For older couples whose children have moved away for work, one partner falling ill can leave the other struggling to coordinate treatment, travel and follow-up visits. The absence of accessible transport and medical services at home can turn routine healthcare into an exhausting exercise.
Shanti, trustee and volunteer at Roshni Trust, which has organised mental health camps in bastis, says Hyderabad’s urban spaces do little to encourage inclusion and social interaction among older people. “The city is designed for isolation and does not promote inclusiveness,” she says.
Shanti calls for government centres at the basti level, on the lines of Anganwadis, where older people can access basic facilities, attend health camps and receive nutritious food. Such centres could also offer a place to meet others, reducing isolation among those who spend much of their time at home.
The search for dependable care
For older people who need help with daily activities, finding a caregiver presents its own difficulties. Volunteers point to the need for people who understand the physical and emotional needs of senior citizens, as well as concerns about safety when elderly couples live alone and their children live elsewhere. Sobha recalls the case of an elderly woman who sleeps during the day and stays awake at night to keep an eye on her caregiver, fearing for her safety.
“This fear weighs on many older people who live with hired help,” she adds.
Through Telangana Stree Seva Samstha, she along with 80-plus volunteers, distributes adult diapers, commode converter seats, walking sticks, books and other resources to those who need them.
S. Bhooma Reddy (78), editor of Voice of Senior Citizens magazine, says the demand for caregivers is substantial, with some families hiring them even when their children live in the same building. “The caregivers are paid a monthly salary of around ₹25,000, apart from being provided food and accommodation,” he adds.
Such arrangements, however, remain beyond the reach of many households. Families from financially disadvantaged backgrounds often live in cramped homes and juggle work, household responsibilities and the care of parents or in-laws with limited resources.
V. Manjula, president of Gruha Karmikula Union-Telangana, says opening community halls where older people are provided regular meals and medicines would be a significant source of support for those from poor backgrounds.
The consequences of inadequate family support can be more severe than the absence of daily assistance. Associations report cases of older people being abandoned at hospitals, railway stations and bus stops. They also cite instances of elderly parents being neglected after transferring property to their children. Physical ailments are not the only problems that can go unnoticed as people grow older. Depression and dementia, too, may remain undiagnosed because their early signs are mistaken for normal aspects of ageing.
K. Chandra Sekhar, 70, founder-director of ASHA Hospitals, says families often seek specialist help only after symptoms have worsened. Forgetfulness, which can be an early sign of dementia, is frequently dismissed as a natural consequence of growing old. Such assumptions can delay diagnosis and prevent older people and their families from accessing appropriate support.
“Early diagnosis can improve quality of life and help caregivers prepare for the support that may be required as a condition progresses,” he says.
A loss of interest in activities once enjoyed, reduced appetite and weight loss, less social interaction and multiple physical complaints can be signs of depression, Dr. Chandra Sekhar points out. Older people experiencing forgetfulness can consult neurologists or psychiatrists.
While health camps often screen for physical illnesses, camps focused on identifying mental health problems are rarely organised, he says.
Aarathi Bellary, consultant physician and co-founder of Aayu Geriatrics, says some older people overlook age-related health problems even when symptoms become apparent.
“While physiological issues get attention, mental health issues in old age are barely discussed. One should not dismiss every problem as an inevitable part of ageing. It is important to consult the relevant medical specialists,” she says.
Dr. Bellary also encourages older people to pursue hobbies, maintain an active social life and take part in activities that allow them to share their knowledge and experience. Such engagement can help them remain socially connected rather than being defined solely by their health needs.
Planning for assisted living
For those who need more sustained support, assisted living and other residential care options could fill a gap between hospital treatment and independent living. Hyderabad, however, has only a few such facilities.
Ambati Rampapa Rao, chairman of PACCS Healthcare Pvt Ltd, which has a subsidiary, Ucchvas Transitional Care Centres, says longer life expectancy has made it necessary to plan for the changing needs of older people, particularly when their children move out of their hometown.
Ageing can bring a range of difficulties, including reduced physical strength, tremors, weight loss, malnutrition and emotional or psychological problems, affecting one’s ability to carry out everyday activities.
Dr. Rao outlines three broad categories of elderly care. Transitional care provides support immediately after hospital discharge, ranging from a few weeks to several years, with some degree of medical supervision; assisted living caters to those whose age and medical history call for monitoring and preventive care; and elderly living facilities serve people who remain mobile but have minor health problems.
“Social and aspirational security has to be factored in while designing spaces for the elderly, to meet their emotional and intellectual aspirations. This has to be planned for people of all financial segments,” he says.
With corporates exploring investments in the sector, the number of facilities could increase. But affordability remains central to whether these services can reach those who need them the most.
Care beyond the family
The Telangana government has sanctioned 37 multi-service daycare centres for senior citizens, of which 32 are operational. Run by non-governmental organisations with full financial support and monitoring from the government, the centres encourage social interaction and provide nutritious food, indoor games and basic medical check-ups once a week.
For older people who depend on regular meals or monitoring of health conditions, however, the reliability of these services matters as much as their availability. One elderly woman says she worries that health problems could jeopardise her access to the centre.
“My sugar levels shoot up if I don’t have food on time. Someone else may develop other health problems. If we fall ill at the centre, our children may consider taking us there a hassle and ask us to stop going,” she says.
Her concern points to a larger dilemma: services intended to support older people may not be enough if families view the time and effort involved in accessing them as a burden.
As Telangana’s elderly population grows, the challenge will be to make care accessible not only to those who can afford paid assistance, but also to people whose health problems, limited mobility or financial circumstances threaten their independence.

briefs.headline: Cabinet Secretary had copied acknowledgement sent to letters by two ECs to CEC for ‘information’: RTI reply
briefs.deck: Election Commissioners S.S. Sandhu and Vivek Joshi wrote to Cabinet Secretary T.V. Somanathan on July 29 regarding the working of Senior Deputy Election Commissioner Maneesh Garg
briefs.bodyText:
Days after two Election Commissioners (ECs) S.S. Sandhu and Vivek Joshi wrote to Cabinet Secretary T.V. Somanathan on July 29 regarding the working of Senior Deputy Election Commissioner Maneesh Garg, the secretariat sent an acknowledgment to both with a copy to Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar for his “information”, a Right to Information (RTI) response has revealed.
The Cabinet Secretariat noted that the letters were from the ECs in their individual capacity and while needed to be taken with seriousness, cannot be taken as formal communication from the Election Commission of India (ECI) as a whole. In the absence of any official communication from the commission any action can be construed as “interference”.
The RTI plea was filed by Commodore (retired) Lokesh Batra.
Work allocation
A Cabinet Secretariat file noting dated August 3 says both the ECs had stated that Mr. Garg, after assuming the charge as link officer of DEC (Administration), issued an order regarding work allocation of equivalent and senior officers to him without discussing the revised work allocation with the commission or the officers concerned. Further, the ECs stated that this happened despite repeated oral and written instructions to all officers against taking such actions without prior discussion/approval of the commission.
“In this connection, we may request the Chief Election Commissioner for his opinion on the issue. Accordingly, a draft D.O. is put up for approval, please,” it said.
However, the very next day, that is August 4, the file notes that “the commission is a constitutional body and is insulated from executive interference by design to ensure that it functions independently and in a transparent manner”.
“The above communications are from the ECs in their individual capacity and, while they must be taken with due seriousness, they cannot be seen as a formal communication from the commission as a whole”.
It further says the ECs have sent these communications for appropriate action. However, “in the absence of any official communication from the commission as a whole, any action at this stage may be inappropriate. It may also be construed as interference in the functioning of the constitutional body”.
And hence, it will be appropriate to send acknowledgement to both ECs with a copy to PPS to the CEC for “information of CEC”.
A copy was also marked to be sent to the Secretary, Department of Personnel and Training since Mr. Garg was an All-India Service officer as well as ACC appointee.
“Draft DO may be put up accordingly”, it said.
Subsequently, on August 5, Mr. Somanathan wrote to both the ECs acknowledging the letters with a copy to PPS to the CEC.
It was though not clear from the RTI responses whether Mr. Gyanesh Kumar had in any manner responded to or acknowledged the information received from the Cabinet Secretariat.

briefs.headline: Indian killed as Houthis attack Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport
briefs.deck: Separately, the Houthis (Ansar Allah) claimed that Saudi Arabia had attacked a yacht carrying Indians in the Red Sea, adding that they were conducting rescue operations
briefs.bodyText:
Two people, including an Indian national, were killed and eight others injured on Wednesday (October 21, 2026) in a Houthi attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Saudi Arabia’s eastern oil hub, the kingdom’s General Authority of Civil Aviation said.
The Indian Embassy in Riyadh confirmed the Indian national’s death. “Saudi authorities have informed that one Indian national was among two people who unfortunately lost their lives in the attack on Dammam airport yesterday night and two Indian nationals were injured,” the Indian embassy wrote in a social media post on Thursday (October 22, 2026). “We are ascertaining further details and contacting the affected families. Our thoughts and prayers are with the family and loved ones of the deceased and we wish speedy recovery of the injured.”
Airport operations and air traffic had returned to normal after brief disruptions, the Saudi aviation authority said.
Separately, the Houthis (Ansar Allah) claimed that Saudi Arabia had attacked a yacht carrying Indians in the Red Sea, adding that they were conducting rescue operations.
The Houthis, who control northern and northwestern Yemen, including the capital, Sana’a, said they launched missile and drone attacks at the Saudi Ministry of Defence in Riyadh and the Dammam airport. They also struck a facility of Aramco, Saudi Arabia’s state-owned petroleum and natural gas company, in Yanbu, and the Abha International Airport in the southwest.
If Saudi Arabia continues to attack Yemen, “we will resort to major options we did not want to take, and we hold it responsible for the consequences,” the militants said, according to the Houthi-aligned Almasirah television.
The Iran-aligned rebels, who captured Sana’a in 2014 and expanded their territorial control along Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast last month, also claimed that the Saudi forces on Thursday targeted an Indian yacht near Zuqar Island in Red Sea, carrying 14 Indians.
“The [Houthi] Armed Forces are carrying out rescue operations for those on board, with further details to be provided later,” they said, according to Almasirah. “It indicated that this reckless behavior by the Saudi enemy threatens international navigation in the Red Sea, requiring the international community to stop the Saudi enemy from these reckless actions.”
The targeting of a civilian vessel carrying Indian nationals raises serious concerns about the safety of international navigation and the potential for civilian casualties, they added.
Saudi Arabia started bombing Yemen in 2015 after the Houthis captured Sana’a a few months earlier. In 2022, Riyadh and the Houthi leadership agreed to a ceasefire as part of a broader Iran-Saudi rapprochement. The ceasefire collapsed in July this year, in the midst of the U.S.-Iran war, as the Sana’a airport was bombed by Saudi Arabia to prevent an Iranian airline carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis then started attacking Saudi Arabia and launched a ground offensive against the Saudi-backed government in Yemen. They have also announced a blockade of Saudi ports in the Red Sea.
In recent weeks, the Houthis have stepped up attacks against Saudi airports and energy infrastructure, while the kingdom has intensified its air strikes on the Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen.
On Thursday (October 22, 2026), the Houthis said they will continue their operations against Saudi Arabia. “There will be siege for siege and escalation for escalation,” they said, adding that the strikes would continue until Saudi Arabia lifts its blockade of the Houthi-held areas of Yemen.

briefs.headline: Face-off with China continues at multiple locations along Arunachal border: ITBP D-G
briefs.deck: ITBP chief says drones are the future of warfare, warning that India cannot face China with traditional weapons alone; says underground shelters are a priority in the new style of border warfare
briefs.bodyText:
Confrontations with Chinese troops continue to take place at multiple sites along the border in Arunachal Pradesh, according to Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) director general Shatrujeet Kapur.
“In the past few-days, a situation arose where face-off happened at several locations in Arunachal and it still continues,” Mr. Kapur said on Thursday.
This is the first official confirmation of the scale of the rising tensions on the north-eastern border since July this year.
Also Read | India, China to push for ‘early and substantial harvest’ of border delimitation
High-altitude commandos
Speaking at the Himveer Samman Samaroah, an annual felicitation ceremony for ITBP personnel, Mr. Kapur said ITBP commandos have been active in the continuing confrontations on the Arunachal border.
“Our newly raised Shaurya commandos played an exemplary role in this. ITBP was raised as a mountain guerilla force and we were given border guarding duty along China in 2004,” he said. “We need not leave our original function, and a specialised high altitude mountain fighting force is being set up, distinct than the army. We will soon have one full battalion of Shaurya commandos; high-altitude [deployment] is our strength,” Mr. Kapur added, during the event held at the Central Training College (CTC), Alwar, Rajasthan.
Also Read | India, China open door to clarifying LAC perceptions
Chinese troops dig in
Government sources told The Hindu that since late July, India and China have been engaged in a stand-off at Asaphila near Taksing in Arunachal Pradesh. The Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) have pitched their tents at an elevation, within 6 km to 7 km of India’s perception of the Line of Actual Control (LAC), near the Maja company operating base in Taksing circle of Upper Subansiri district, sources said.
“Sometime in July, during routine patrolling, Indian and Chinese troops came face to face near Maja. After brief confrontation, both sides returned but the Chinese PLA came back in larger number few days later and pitched tents, around 6-7 kms within India’s perception of the LAC,” the source said.
India has also increased deployment along the border.
Border talks
The situation has persisted even though Chinese President Xi Jinping attended the 18th BRICS Summit hosted by India from September 11 to 13, and the two nations have held three high-level border talks since July.
The 36th WMCC (Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs) meeting on India-China border affairs was held on August 6. This was followed by the 25th round of talks between the Special Representatives (SR) on the Boundary Question on August 26 in Beijing, where India was represented by National Security Adviser (NSA) Ajit Doval. On September 6, the first-ever Corps Commander-level meetings between the two armies was held in the Eastern Sector at the Vacha-Damai Border Personnel Meeting Point in Arunachal Pradesh. Such meetings have so far largely been held at the Chushul-Moldo Border Meeting Point in eastern Ladakh, particularly after the Galwan Valley clashes in June 2020.
The Army and the ITBP force are deployed along the China border and long range patrols are regularly sent to the forward areas. Due to the weather conditions, such patrols are sent between June and October in Arunachal Pradesh.
Also Read | China’s media slams India’s move of formally naming 27 places in Arunachal Pradesh
‘Drone tech is key’
The weapons used by the ITBP are 50-years old and modernisation is required, said Mr. Kapur, who is set to retire on October 31. Stressing on the need to invest and develop drone and counter-drone technology, the ITBP chief said that it may not be possible to face China through traditional methods as it has invested a lot in the modernisation of its weapons and infrastructure.
“Drones are something through which a even a small country can challenge a big country We saw how Ukraine has challenged a superpower like Russia. The war was supposed to be over in few days, but 10,000 to 15,000 Russian soldiers are being killed, they are suffering. Look at Iran, how, without even a Navy, they, with the help of drones, challenged America,” he said.
“We have to go towards drones and anti-drone systems. We spent 70% of ₹400 crore modernisation funds on drones. There is one drone platoon in all border guarding battalions, we have started training drone pilots, we are making drones in-house. Out of another modernisation scheme of ₹3,500 to ₹4,000 crore, ₹1,000 crore have been earmarked for drones,” said Mr. Kapur.
Also Read | Peace in border areas of ‘utmost importance’, says MEA after reports of Chinese incursions
‘Underground shelters are priority’
Mr. Kapur added that a decision has been taken to build as many underground shelters as those above the ground along the China border, over the next three years. “Underground shelters are key to new warfare. Anything overground can be a target. In hot-war situations, underground shelters are a priority,” he said.
“All companies have started pilot projects on building underground structures, which will act as permanent defences. They should be comfortable, with adequate bathrooms, ventilation, drainage. Once the design is final through a pilot project, every border outpost will have the same number of overground and underground structure in the next three years. It will protect us in any war situation,” he said.

briefs.headline: The grandmothers hitting patriarchy and weights
briefs.deck: Grandmothers in areas surrounding Delhi are rewriting the rules of engagement, one reel at a time. From challenging patriarchy and lifting weights to dancing to Haryanvi pop and inspiring other seniors to embrace fitness, they are turning social media into a platform for self-expression, defiance, and a new-found freedom, finds Ashok Kumar
briefs.bodyText:
Period blood is the only blood that does not flow because of violence. “Still, society despises that blood the most.” Savitri Hooda, 65, speaks straight into her phone camera, standing under a neem tree in her home’s backyard. That video, shot from Rohtak’s Mungan village, 70 km north-west of Delhi, got 19,000 ‘likes’ on Instagram.
In another reel, she looks at the camera and calls her own generation “shoddy”. “Should I list their misdeeds? They killed daughters in the womb, discriminated against their own daughters, burnt their daughters-in-law for dowry, and leered at other women. They treated women as second-class citizens and now cannot stand their freedom.” That got her 4,87,000 likes and a whole lot of comments from people showering love on “Dadi”.
Welcome to @tai_savitri’s month-old Instagram account, which has just 27 posts but 3,08,000 followers. Her bio says: “Desi feminist from Haryana. Freedom and unfiltered opinions.”
The overwhelming response to her profile has been startling even for the family. Her son, Ashish, recalls receiving the first podcast invitation when Savitri had around 3,000 followers. After her video on mental health went viral last month, interview requests began pouring in.
Across the National Capital Region (NCR), women over 60 are putting their voices out on social media. They are singing, dancing, and giving out wisdom that the youth is lapping up.
The irreverent feminist
For Savitri, speaking her mind is hardly new. The rebellious streak that now finds an audience online surfaced when she was a schoolgirl. She dropped out in Class 7 after her mother, whom she describes as “very conservative”, refused to let her participate in a school play about dowry and opposed her taking up judo as well. “She thought it would disgrace the family. So I quit my studies in protest,” Savitri says.
It is a decision she still regrets.
Her formal education may have ended early, but Ashish says his mother has always been receptive to new ideas. She listens, reflects, and frequently brings her own observations into discussions, sometimes surprising the family with the connections she makes.
Her curiosity has also translated into considerable digital independence. Savitri records and uploads videos, manages her YouTube account and responds to comments herself. She uses the voice-to-text tool because it is faster than entering text manually. “If someone writes in English and I cannot understand the comment, I reply, ‘Thank you for sharing your views’,” she says.
To meet her is to meet an anti-influencer. She sits cross-legged on a bed in a dimly lit room, plaster peeling off its green-painted walls. Clothes hang shabbily on pegs. Ashish, an aspiring stand-up comic and novelist, leaning against a pillow beside her. She asks her husband to make three cups of tea. “What is the point in talking about feminism if I cannot finish patriarchy at my own house?” she says, chuckling.
Her social media journey started as a son’s sentimental plan during COVID-19. “He said it would preserve my memories. That the children could watch their grandmother singing folk songs when they grew up,” Savitri says, as her grandson sits by her. “I was fond of singing, so I agreed. That channel, ‘Yo Apna Haryana’, renamed ‘Tai Savitri’, now has 3,31,000 subscribers and 14,000 videos. But singing felt hollow after her singing partner lost her 28-year-old son in an accident. So she quit.
“When the singing stopped, we had to think about what to do next,” says Ashish, who has a postgraduate degree in Zoology. The answer emerged from conversations at home.
Ashish had developed an interest in theatre, philosophy, and psychology over the years. So, discussions about ideas and society were a regular feature of family life.
Ashish says that he does not quote philosophers word for word to his mother. Instead, he translates them into everyday language, allowing discussions to unfold at home over days or even weeks before they eventually find expression in a video.
It led to her creating videos on feminism and against social evils.
Bertrand Russell’s proposition that people should need a licence to become parents, for instance, prompted a conversation that led to one of Savitri’s most-watched videos on parenting. At other times, the starting point is something she observes in society or among people around her. “The videos are not scripted. If I get her to deliver it as a script, she won’t be able to speak with the same conviction,” says the 27-year-old.
After a mental health video went viral, the family received an anonymous call from a man who threatened to kill Savitri. “That was the first time I was genuinely frightened,” says Ashish.
Her criticism of local godmen in her videos has also drawn displeasure. The backlash has not been confined to anonymous callers. A khap leader once called on his father, Bijender Singh Hooda, to complain. “He said my father had removed the nath — the nose rope — from his wife. He was comparing a woman to an animal controlled by a nose rope,” he says.
Savitri, meanwhile, draws inspiration from watching godman-philosopher Osho and civil services exam coach Vikas Divyakirti. Her subjects have expanded from feminism to mental health and Gen Z, but Ashish says there is no deliberate strategy behind the transition. The themes emerge naturally from what they see and discuss around them. But she is not done. “Whether people throw flowers at me or slippers, I am going to debut as a stand-up comedian soon. My son is writing it for me,” she announces. And she wants a passport stamp. “I have seen enough of Haryana, now I want to go abroad. I don’t have money. If someone sponsors me, I would like to travel to Australia and the U.S.,” she says, deadpan.
The dancing dadi
More than 100 km from Savitri Hooda’s village in Rohtak, in a crowded lane of Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh, Birvati, 85, another woman is blowing up the idea of age-appropriate. Yellow tee, brown pants, two pigtails, the unlettered dadi (paternal grandmother) breaks into a Haryanvi pop number —‘Mera Balam Thanedar’— with the energy of a teenager.
She has 5,36,000 views with just that one video. Her handle on Instagram, dadi_comedy_63, has 230 posts and is less than a year old, with 1,16,000 followers already. Her son Kiranpal sells artificial jewellery, at weekly markets. These days, he says, the market comes to them. “People now recognise her. When we go to the market, people come and sit beside her and say, ‘Amma, look how well your videos are doing!’ There is so much excitement. People ask her, ‘Amma, where did you learn all this? You do it so well!’” he says, proudly.
Birvati, with white hair and wrinkled skin, plays humble, but knows her influence. “I don’t like praising myself, but there is hardly anyone who has not seen my videos. People, not just in India, but even abroad are getting to know me,” she says with a toothless grin.
“Women my age tell me, ‘Amma, you have done something remarkable at this age. You have made a name!’” she adds.
Her granddaughter Neha says people are pulled in by her energy.
“The dance moves she does are rare for people her age. Most people are fascinated by her energy,” says the 20-year-old, who is Birvati’s choreographer, costume designer, and editor. “She wears different outfits for songs, rarely a sari. She experiments with hairstyles, and even asks me, ‘Can I go out wearing jeans?’”
But this wasn’t supposed to be Birvati’s channel. It was Neha’s. She has a degree in optometry and wanted to create online content. Her parents said no, afraid of facing a problem finding groom for a girl who is popular online. So Neha brought in her grandmother, who had been the life and soul of every family wedding in her youth, to dance with her. They started in December last year, with a YouTube channel called ‘Neha Panchal’, posting dance and humorous videos, both dadi and granddaughter in frame. Their first video got a like from singer Neha Kakkar. That was enough to keep going. Instagram came a month later. And it exploded. Younger audience, more likes, more engagement. “Whenever I tell her we are shooting, she gets ready an hour in advance. She is more excited than I am. She gets dressed on her own. Sometimes she chooses the song herself. Some videos on the rooftop, some in the park outside, and some on the middle floor. I have decorated a corner for this,” Neha says.
“In the beginning, the comments were brutal. “At this age, do bhajans, not dances. Go to the temple,” people wrote. Neha’s batchmates laughed at her, saying she was unnecessarily dragging her grandmother in. She ignored them. Now the whole family is involved. Neha’s mother, Poonam, once hooked to Hindi novels, is the scriptwriter for their comedy sketches. “She reads stories, watches things, and comes up with ideas.” Older sister Riya also pops in.
Birvati wants to contribute financially. Neha says Punjabi singers have approached them for paid promotions, but the income is still small and unsteady. But Birvati wants to grow into her newfound career and make her own songs. “I want a role in a Haryanvi music video,” she says.
Dare to deadlift
Cut from a 50 sq. ft. house in Ghaziabad to a plush plotted house in South City-I, Gurugram. Amrit Kaur, 75, sits gracefully on a beige tufted sofa, hands folded neatly in her lap, composed, almost stern. Four years ago, she could barely walk. “I have always been strong. But four years ago, I became seriously ill. I was very weak, and was admitted in hospital,” she recalls. “I thought I would recover in a few days, but the weakness was considerable.” Today she does an hour of strength training at 4 a.m. every day.
She can do a dozen push-ups.
Her Instagram handle, @getfitwithdadi, has just 40 posts, 17,000 followers and a video with 80 lakh views. Her son, Aminder Singh, sits beside her. In his early 50s, Singh is the founder of Team Aminder, and has been training people for 30 years, with clients in 42 countries. “She was very weak after hospital. But I used to tell her, ‘Mummy, you are very strong,’” he says.
He made her start small. Tie a rope between door frames. Pull it. Do a squat. Again.
“At first, I could do very little. But slowly, I began to feel that I was regaining some strength,” Amrit says, who was reluctant to start.
Amrit begins her day at 3 or 3:30 a.m. with prayers. “Then I begin exercising,” she says. “I keep chanting ‘Waheguru, Satnam, Waheguru, Satnam’ as I squat. My prayers and exercise go on together. Gradually, I increased the time. Now I exercise for an hour.”
Commentaires pour in. “You have done something wonderful, Dadi! You are amazing!” says one. She reads them, but doesn’t reply. “I feel particularly happy when others imitate me. I feel the exercises I do are useful to others,” she says. At the nearby gurdwara, devotees now recognise her as: “Arre, video wali dadi (Oh, the grandmother from the video)!” Taking a cue from Amrit, Aminder’s mother-in-law Deepa Bindra has started her own handle @getfitwithnaani, with seven posts and 3,916 followers already. Amrit has a message that isn’t about protein: “Exercise is effective only if we are happy.”

Two men returning from Mysuru after attending the Dasara festivities died after their motorcycle allegedly rammed into a roadside electric pole near Mylasandra Junction in east Bengaluru’s Kengeri on Friday.

The incident unfolded around 2.30 a.m., according to the police. A preliminary police probe revealed that eight people on four two-wheelers had travelled to Mysuru to watch the Dasara festivities.

Overspeeding suspected
