stories.headline: This weekend, Bengaluru stages stories of belonging and memory
stories.bodyText:
What makes a place home? Is it the memories we carry, the people we find, or the freedom to belong without boundaries? These questions take centre stage at the 
Ranga Shankara Theatre Festival (RSTF) 2026
, which runs from October 23 to 31 under the theme 
Belonging: Through Memory, Migration and Boundaries
. Bringing together six productions in Hindi, Ladakhi, Haryanavi, Malayalam, Bengali and English, the festival has been curated by five young theatre practitioners from across the city. It explores how people negotiate identity, displacement and their relationship with home.
‘Belonging is about how we make room for one another’
Sushma Rao, one of the curators, says Bengaluru’s diverse population makes the theme particularly relevant. People arrive carrying different languages, memories and ideas of home, but belonging is about more than finding one’s place in a new city. “Ultimately, belonging is not just about finding a home for ourselves; it is also about how we make room for one another,” she says.
‘Bengaluru is a city that has assimilated people who have arrived’
Sneha Kappanna points to the contrast between the city’s openness and its divisions. “Bengaluru is a city that has assimilated people who have arrived. Every new arrival brings a story, a culture, a language and a set of memories,” she says, adding that there is also “stark isolation and suffocating fragmentation”. She believes theatre offers a powerful way to examine who belongs and how people can cross over into another person’s world.
‘We always wanted to highlight how broad the idea of belonging is’
The festival’s six productions approach the theme through different experiences. Utthana Barighat, who worked on the programme, says, “The theme ranges from the impact of climate change and political borders to the deeply personal experience of losing one’s memories. We always wanted to highlight how broad the idea of belonging is.”
‘Without a collective sense of solidarity, none of us will survive’
For Surabhi Herur, the open call for applications reveals how widely the theme resonates. “Love, longing and care came up over and over again,” she says, adding that the plays underline how easily the right to belong can be taken away. She hopes audiences leave recognising the importance of solidarity across differences.
‘Live theatre offers a sense of community that streaming cannot’
“Streaming movies at home is easy, but it is completely different from sitting in a crowded hall watching a play live,” says Vinay Shastry, another of the five curators. “On stage, actors are right there in front of you — sweating, laughing and pouring their hearts out in real time, and you feel every bit of that energy.” He believes this shared experience is what sets theatre apart from digital entertainment, bringing strangers together through laughter, emotion and excitement.
Beyond the performances, the festival features poetry readings, conversations on language and memory, letters from across the world, and interactive stations where visitors can share stories about home, food, migration and kindness.

briefs.headline: Karnataka to frame policy against hospitals withholding bodies over unpaid bills
briefs.deck: Health Minister U.T. Khader says no hospital should deny families the bodies of deceased patients; government to examine complaints of excessive billing
briefs.bodyText:
Karnataka’s Health Department will formulate a clear policy to prevent hospitals from withholding the bodies of deceased patients over unpaid medical bills, Health Minister U.T. Khader said on Thursday.
Speaking after a meeting with representatives of the Private Hospitals and Nursing Homes Association (PHANA) in Bengaluru, Mr. Khader said no patient or family should be subjected to financial pressure during a medical emergency and that hospitals should not deny families access to the bodies of deceased patients on account of pending dues.
The Health Department would frame a policy to address the issue, he said, reiterating that patient welfare and affordable healthcare remained the State government’s priorities.
The meeting also discussed measures to curb excessive billing by private hospitals, regulate the prices of essential medicines, and improve transparency in medical charges. Further decisions on allegations of exorbitant billing would be taken after consultations with officials, Mr. Khader said.
Measures to regulate medicine prices
Discussions will be held with pharmaceutical manufacturers and distributors to address the high prices of essential medicines, particularly those used in cancer, cardiac, and kidney care, the Minister said.
Citing instances of substantial differences between the cost of medicines and the prices charged to patients, he said the department had undertaken an exercise to ascertain the actual landing costs of drugs. He referred to cases in which injections costing ₹5,000 to ₹6,000 were reportedly being sold for as much as ₹65,000. He said the department had undertaken an exercise to ascertain the actual landing costs of medicines and examine the margins charged along the supply chain.
While scheduled drugs are subject to regulated price controls, concerns persist over the prices charged for certain medicines. The government would hold discussions with pharmaceutical manufacturers and distributors to address excessive mark-ups, particularly on medicines used in cancer, cardiac, and kidney care, and to prevent unauthorised increases in maximum retail prices (MRP).
“We are also contemplating asking the pharma companies to print the actual landing costs and MRP on the medicine strips,” he said.
Mr. Khader also reiterated that hospitals should display the rates of major procedures prominently from November 1. Hospitals offering a large number of services should maintain detailed rate cards at their reception counters for public scrutiny.
Insurance billing under scrutiny
The government would convene a separate meeting with insurance companies to address complaints of excessive billing for insured patients and simplify the claims settlement process, the Minister said.
The meeting with private hospitals also addressed regulatory concerns relating to the Fire Department, the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board, and the Karnataka Private Medical Establishments (KPME) Act. The government would examine the representations received and take appropriate steps, he added.
Concerns over foreign investment in healthcare
The Health Minister raised concerns over the growing commercialisation of healthcare and the implications of foreign investment in corporate hospital chains.
He indicated that the State government would take up the issue with the Union government to explore whether foreign investments in the healthcare sector should be restricted or subjected to stricter price controls.
The issue comes amid concerns over the rising cost of private healthcare and the financial burden on patients. Any further steps in this regard would require consultations with the Union government and consideration of the applicable regulatory framework, he added.

briefs.headline: Two more on police radar in suspected IED blast in Bengaluru
briefs.bodyText:
Two more individuals are on the police radar in connection with the blast at an under-construction building in Pulakeshinagar in east Bengaluru, which is suspected to have been triggered by an Improvised Explosive Device (IED).
A senior police officer said the two individuals are suspected of having played a role in the logistics, including the delivery of materials believed to have been used in assembling the suspected IED.
Meanwhile, the Pulakeshinagar police have registered a case under Sections 61 (criminal conspiracy) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and Sections 3 and 5 of the Explosive Substances Act, 1908. These provisions deal with causing an explosion likely to endanger life or property and possessing explosive substances under suspicious circumstances.
A senior police officer told The Hindu that the police suspected an IED, citing remnants, including wires, was recovered from the scene. The blast was allegedly triggered after a torch button was pressed.
However, the police maintain that the nature of the material can be established only after the Forensic Science Laboratory report is received.
One severely injured
According to a senior police officer, one of the two injured persons – Allauddin from Assam and Suraj from Uttar Pradesh – is being questioned by the police. Allauddin, the officer said, has suffered a severe eye injury and is likely to lose vision in one eye.
Meanwhile, the Bengaluru police have contacted their counterparts in Assam and Uttar Pradesh to verify the antecedents of both the injured. Another senior officer said that neither of them had any criminal cases registered against them in Karnataka.
“Both are working in the city through a contractor and keep visiting their native places. We are verifying their backgrounds and previous whereabouts,” he said.
It is also learnt that an investigator from the National Investigation Agency has joined the city police as the investigation continues.

briefs.headline: Bengaluru Pink Line Metro opening approval expected within five days; Blue Line trial runs by October-end
briefs.deck: The announcements came as the Minister reviewed the progress of Metro construction and directed officials to accelerate work on the delayed Blue Line corridor connecting KR Puram with Hebbal and Kempegowda International Airport
briefs.bodyText:
Trial runs on the K.R. Puram-Central Silk Board stretch of Namma Metro’s Blue Line are scheduled to begin by the end of October, while the elevated section of the Pink Line is expected to receive approval for passenger operations within the next four to five days, Minister for Greater Bengaluru Development Krishna Byre Gowda said on Thursday.
The announcements came as the Minister reviewed the progress of the metro construction and directed officials to accelerate work on the delayed Blue Line corridor connecting K.R. Puram with Hebbal and Kempegowda International Airport.
According to Mr. Gowda, the 7.5-km elevated section of the Pink Line, between Kalena Agrahara and Tavarekere, has completed its trial runs.
“Safety and electrical tests have also been conducted over the past seven to eight months. The remaining step is official clearance to commence passenger services,” he said.
The State government has written to the Union government and the Ministers concerned, requesting an early decision on the inauguration date.
Mr. Gowda said that the Chief Minister’s letter was yet to get a response and indicated that he would seek a meeting with the Union Minister concerned to expedite the process.
Blue Line construction faces delays
During his inspection of the construction sites, Mr. Gowda said that the Blue Line corridors under the Metro Phases 2A and 2B were crucial to Bengaluru’s transport infrastructure. However, construction between K.R. Puram, Nagawara and Hebbal has encountered several obstacles, pushing the project at least a year beyond its scheduled timeline.
The work near K.R. Puram was delayed for approximately a year due to a court stay on tree-felling.
The Minister said the process of obtaining approvals for tree removal in Bengaluru involved multiple stages, including proceedings before the Tree Committee and the High Court.
The relocation of Cauvery water supply pipelines and underground drainage infrastructure has also affected the construction, particularly along the Veerannapalya-Hebbal stretch. According to the Minister, shifting existing utilities and laying replacement lines caused delays of around six to eight months.
Heavy traffic on the Outer Ring Road has further restricted construction activities, forcing workers to carry out much of the work between 7 p.m. and the early hours of the morning, he added.
While acknowledging the difficulties associated with large infrastructure projects, Mr. Gowda claimed that contractors had not worked at the required pace. He directed the officials to ensure that no further delays occur and pressed them to accelerate construction.
Train operations targeted for next year
The K.R. Puram-Central Silk Board corridor, measuring 19.75 km, is expected to see trains operating progressively along individual station sections from the first week of November. The immediate objective is to extend operations towards Marathahalli, with commercial services between K.R. Puram and Central Silk Board targeted for around the middle of next year.
“The 38.44-km K.R. Puram-Kempegowda International Airport corridor is also under construction. The government aims to begin train operations on the Hebbal-airport stretch by October or November next year. The officials have been directed to initiate trial runs in the first week of November and accelerate work towards Marathahalli or Hebbal,” Mr. Gowda said.
Meanwhile, the Minister instructed the officials to remove construction barricades from sections of the Outer Ring Road where the metro work has been completed, restoring road space for traffic.
Mr. Gowda said that the combined expansion of the metro, suburban rail and bus services could address up to 50% of Bengaluru’s traffic problems once the measures become operational over the next one to two years.

stories.headline: At €310 billion, Union minister Piyush Goyal eyes 10x rise in Indo-German trade
stories.deck: At the inauguration of the India Centre and Indo-German Business Forum in Berlin, Goyal said the FTA could be signed by Dec and implemented within four to five months. “We had 31.5 billion euros (in 2025) and (if) we were to be able to add a zero to that, make it 310 billion euros. How would that sound? Now, we can certainly make that happen,” he said, emphasising the need to draw up concrete…
stories.bodyText:
BERLIN: Commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal Thursday set an ambitious target of increasing bilateral trade with Germany tenfold to 310 billion euros, urging businesses to forge partnerships ahead of implementation of the India-EU free trade agreement (FTA).
At the inauguration of the India Centre and Indo-German Business Forum in Berlin, Goyal said the FTA could be signed by Dec and implemented within four to five months. “We had 31.5 billion euros (in 2025) and (if) we were to be able to add a zero to that, make it 310 billion euros. How would that sound? Now, we can certainly make that happen,” he said, emphasising the need to draw up concrete plans to realise the ambition.
Goyal is on a visit to Germany and the Netherlands from Oct 22 to 27, leading a delegation of around 100 Indian businesses and startups to explore opportunities in trade, investment and industrial cooperation. The minister said Germany’s precision engineering and commitment to quality complemented India’s infrastructure expansion, digital capabilities and young, skilled workforce, creating scope for collaboration in manufacturing, technology and supply chains. He said the two countries had little to compete with each other and could together strengthen supply chain resilience and have a transformational impact on each other’s economies.
He asked businesses to start identifying customers and investors, exploring partnerships and aligning product quality and pricing with market requirements rather than wait for the FTA to come into effect. “This is the time partnerships need to be forged. This is the time connects need to be made with potential customers, collaborators, investors,” Goyal said, adding that companies must prepare to “trade, invest smarter, faster and get the best out of this agreement”.
Negotiations for the India-EU FTA concluded in Jan this year following talks between PM Narendra Modi and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Goyal said the agreement had received unanimous support from all 27 EU member states and expressed confidence that the remaining process would move rapidly. India-EU trade stood at 118 billion euros in 2025.
Goyal outlined priorities for India and Germany, including strengthening economic security, creating industrial opportunities through the green transition and advancing emerging technologies. He called for closer cooperation in apprenticeships and skilling, areas in which Germany has considerable expertise.
Germany’s minister for economic affairs and energy, Katherina Reiche, said bilateral trade remained below potential, with India not featuring among Germany’s top 20 trading partners despite goods trade worth around 31 billion euros in 2025.
“We could at least double the trade amount we have right now,” she said, calling for greater investment and industrial partnerships. Reiche said German companies had an investment stock of over 28 billion euros in India and that the proposed German-Indian CEO forum was expected to bring business leaders together and encourage fresh investments.
Speaking at Berlin Global Dialogue, Goyal said the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) could hurt European industries. “If you put a CBAM on yourself and put a 50% import duty to bring steel into your country, you are inviting disaster. Your cost of living will go up, your people will be unhappy, your industry will be outpriced.”

stories.headline: eMudhra to exit global SSL/TLS business, shares tank
stories.deck: The company’s board decided to withdraw from the business after reviewing its commercial prospects and the scrutiny triggered by the incident. The global SSL/TLS business contributes about 1% of eMudhra’s revenue, but rising compliance requirements, increasing costs and competition from free certificate providers have reduced its potential returns, the company said.
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: Shares of digital trust company eMudhra plunged 20% on BSE for the second consecutive day on Thursday after it announced its decision to exit the global SSL/TLS (Secure Sockets Layer/Transport Layer Security) certificate business following a security incident involving eight of its intermediate certificate authorities.
The company’s board decided to withdraw from the business after reviewing its commercial prospects and the scrutiny triggered by the incident. The global SSL/TLS business contributes about 1% of eMudhra’s revenue, but rising compliance requirements, increasing costs and competition from free certificate providers have reduced its potential returns, the company said.
“The scrutiny was disproportionate to the revenue contribution of the business,” Kaushik Srinivasan, co-founder of eMudhra, told TOI, explaining the board’s decision. He said the board met on Thursday to assess the business’s future following the incident and the sharp fall in the company’s share price over the past two sessions.
Investors were bearish on the eMudhra stock after the cyber incident. In two sessions since the incident, its stock price has crashed 36% to Rs 345 by Thursday’s close, from Rs 539 at Monday’s close.
The issue was reported on Oct 17 by Dennis Jackson, a member of Mozilla’s cryptography engineering team, who flagged weaknesses in the keys associated with the eight eMudhra intermediate certificates.
Srinivasan said the economics of the business were becoming less attractive as certificate validity periods shortened. “The return on investment, considering the effort, investment and compliance requirements, is becoming less attractive. It makes more sense to strengthen and invest in our enterprise solutions business, which has higher margins and greater potential,” he said.

stories.headline: eMudhra to exit overseas web security certificate business as stock takes beating
stories.deck: The firm is reeling from eight web security certificates’ private keys being exposed, an incident that could leave out-of-date devices vulnerable to sites using forged security certificates.
stories.bodyText:
eMudhra Ltd., whose intermediate security certificates’ private keys were exposed on Tuesday in an extraordinary security incident, will exit the global business for offering web security certificates, the firm announced on Thursday, after the firm’s stocks hit the circuit breaker for two trading sessions. The incident may have wide-ranging consequences, since eight web security certificates can now be issued by attackers that seem legitimate to devices that have not received updates to distrust them.
The firm will continue the business that it is engaged in for issuance of SSL certificates for Indian websites, a spokesperson for the firm told The Hindu.
The firm said that web security certificates issued for non-Indian subscribers accounted for less than 1% of their revenue but was causing a disproportionate amount of reputational loss for the company, which lost more than a third of its market value in the 48 hours after word of the incident went public. eMudhra’s web and document signing technologies are used all over government and private industry. The IT Ministry has constituted a committee to look into the incident.
Kaushik Srinivasan, eMudhra’s co-founder, told The Hindu in an interview on Thursday before the firm announced the exit, that “perception threats have arisen” for the firm following the incident. “This is a one-off incident on a bad day,” Mr. Srinivasan insisted. “A script error can happen to anybody, right? The key lesson for us is, it’s more like once bitten, twice shy. Therefore, we will obviously put in place rigorous operational security controls.”
“We have not seen any significant negative feedback from any one of them, and we are quite deeply humbled by the support that we are getting from our customers,” Mr. Srinivasan said.
An independent firm not involved with past audits that failed to spot the weak intermediate certificates would be appointed for a review of the firm’s security practices, Mr. Srinivasan said.
Mr. Srinivasan shrugged off concerns that forged certificates based on eMudhra’s exposed private keys could be used in cyberattacks on smart devices. “Smart devices generally rely on certificates that are more private trust, not as much on public trust,” he said. “None of the use cases that we served on smart devices relied on any kind of public trust certificates.”
eMudhra has replied to queries by the IT Ministry’s committee, and will continue to engage with them, Mr. Srinivasan added.

stories.headline: E-rickshaw battery ‘hacks’ and Bluetooth BMS vulnerabilities | Explained
stories.deck: Here’s how Bluetooth BMS actually works, and why the real issue is design vulnerabilities, not “hacks”, but systems built without proper authentication or security in mind
stories.bodyText:
The story so far: Over the last week, social media has been flooded with videos depicting individuals using mobile applications such as BAT-BMS, Lossigy and Epoch-i-ion to wirelessly disable the batteries of e-rickshaws using Bluetooth. The videos have largely been shared as “pranks” — however cruel, unethical and unlawful they may be — while some have speculated that the applications were designed for high-tech sabotage by China’s manufacturers. The reality is far less dramatic, yet still worth understanding carefully.
How battery management systems are diagnosed?
Applications such as BAT-BMS exist to allow fleet owners and service technicians to easily diagnose battery problems such as overvoltage or undervoltage. In most vehicles, battery management and diagnostics require physical access to the module and the use of a computer or other device to gather information.
Over time, manufacturers have begun equipping these modules with Bluetooth capabilities, making diagnostics and repairs easier without requiring extensive disassembly. Applications such as BAT-BMS are typically developed alongside the battery management systems they support and are almost certainly not intended to sow chaos by disabling as many vehicles as possible. Instead, they search for specific devices advertising themselves as battery management modules over Bluetooth, connect to one device at a time, display diagnostic information, and provide basic debugging functions.
Looking under the hood: How e-rickshaws are built and why imported electronics matter?
The BAT-BMS application is specifically designed to discover and connect to BMS modules manufactured by a Chinese electronics company, Jiabaida. A seven-year-old public discussion on the open source code sharing platform GitHub documented a lack of authentication in Jiabaida BMS modules, with the author even providing a hacky workaround for this obvious security flaw.
Over time, this vulnerability appears to have been discovered and subsequently exploited by individuals who began popularising its misuse. In particular, some users circulated short-form “prank” videos demonstrating how it could be used to disable e-rickshaw batteries.
Almost all of the components that make up e-rickshaws are imported from China. In fact, one could order almost all the parts required to assemble one from consumer websites such as Alibaba Group or AliExpress.
When technology is blamed for system vulnerabilities
It appears that whenever something goes wrong, the government is quick enough to attribute blame to digital platforms. Telegram was ordered to be blocked during the Re-NEET period, reportedly to protect individuals from fraudsters claiming to sell leaked examination question papers in advance. Similarly, following viral “prank” incidents, the government directed Google and Apple to remove several popular battery management apps from their respective app stores.
In both cases, the government has chosen to restrict access to applications rather than address the underlying issues in a meaningful way. While the two applications are fundamentally different — one being a widely used communication platform with social media features, and the other a set of utilities for diagnosing battery issues — the reasoning behind both decisions appears similar. In essence, when a particular technology becomes associated with harm, restricting access to that technology is seen as a way to eliminate the harm itself.
Hypothetically, if the Re-NEET examination were to be compromised, the breach would have to occur at the source or during transit — during question formulation, printing, or transport. The breach would not originate from, nor be enabled by, the Telegram platform itself. Blocking Telegram in this hypothetical scenario would only temporarily disrupt the sale of leaked question papers, until sellers migrate to another platform of choice. Similarly, restricting battery management applications does not make vulnerable BMS modules any more secure. If anything, it might further inconvenience users who have been affected and are trying to restore functionality to their vehicles.
How should supply chain regulation be structured?
Contrary to popular belief, regulatory frameworks governing e-rickshaws do exist. Gazette notifications GSR 709(E) dated 8.10.2014 and S.O. 2590(E) dated 8.10.2014 define requirements related to overall dimensions, tyres, brakes, horns, and vehicle identification number standards, but do not provide detailed standards for electronic components.
Globally, as security risks become increasingly associated with the supply chains, various strategies have been adopted to address vulnerabilities before a product reaches the assembly line. These include vetting suppliers, auditing the firmware of electronic components, and tracing the origin and capabilities of individual parts. Such measures can be mandated through regulation. A simple Google search conducted seven years ago could have alerted e-rickshaw manufacturers to the security issues in the BMS modules they use.
Frameworks that establish standards, as well as responsibilities and liabilities for manufacturers, should ideally extend to all products containing electronic components, not just vehicles or specifically e-rickshaws. While sourcing parts from the cheapest available source might be suitable for building a quick prototype, the long-term production and marketing of products should require greater effort and due diligence than simply placing a few orders and setting up an assembly line.
(Karan is an independent security researcher from New Delhi, India.)

briefs.headline: Yes Bank Additional Tier 1 bondholders seek interest payment
briefs.deck: The YES Bank AT1 Retail Bond Holders Association cited Companies Act and Sebi obligations in seeking an explanation for non-payment of the 9% bond coupon due Oct 18, three days after the Oct 15 court order restoring the bonds. It also demanded payment of coupons skipped in 2020-25 and arrangements for the forthcoming Dec 23 coupon on 9.5% bonds.
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Retail bondholders of YES Bank have asked Axis Trustee Services, the debenture trustee, to secure payment of overdue coupons (interest payments) on the bank’s Additional Tier 1 (AT1) bonds, restore their holdings in demat accounts and seek regulatory intervention, days after Supreme Court dismissed appeals against Bombay high court’s ruling that quashed the March 2020 write-off.
The YES Bank AT1 Retail Bond Holders Association cited Companies Act and Sebi obligations in seeking an explanation for non-payment of the 9% bond coupon due Oct 18, three days after the Oct 15 court order restoring the bonds. It also demanded payment of coupons skipped in 2020-25 and arrangements for the forthcoming Dec 23 coupon on 9.5% bonds.
According to analysts, revisiting past coupons raises legal and accounting issues. The write-off was recognised in profit and loss, so restoring the bonds could affect past profits. Coupon payments on high-risk AT1 bonds are also contingent on the bank’s financial performance.
The association asked Axis Trustee to disclose YES Bank’s position on each missed coupon, cancellation notices and correspondence since March 2020, including any reliance on contractual discretion or record dates. It also sought coordination with the bank, registrars NSDL and CDSL in order to restore demat holdings.
Citing the apex court’s observations that AT1 bonds are high-risk instruments meant for institutional investors, despite YES Bank selling them to individuals, the association sought intervention by RBI and markets regulator Sebi.

briefs.headline: Jio IPO subscribed over 5x as institutions bid big
briefs.deck: At the close of Day 2, the total demand for Jio shares was worth about Rs 3.7 lakh crore, including the anchor portion. briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: The maiden public offering for Jio Platforms, through which the company is raising Rs 30,213 crore, making it the largest such offer in India, was subscribed over five times at the close of bidding on Day 2. Institutional investors continued to lead the bidding process—that had helped the IPO to get fully subscribed within the first 100 minutes of opening on Day 1—with high-net-worth investors (HNIs) following closely, data from the bourses showed.
The retail portion of the offer—that was subscribed 70% on Day 1—was also fully subscribed on Thursday, with the Day 2 closing data showing 1.5 times subscription for 8.5 crore shares that are on offer.
At the close of Day 2, the total demand for Jio shares was worth about Rs 3.7 lakh crore, including the anchor portion. On Thursday, the institutional (QIB) part of the IPO, in which a little over 4.9 crore shares were offered, was subscribed nearly 13.3 times, while the HNI portion, in which about 3.6 crore shares were reserved, was subscribed six times. Usually, in most IPOs, institutional players apply on the last day of the offer.
Exchange data also showed that the portion reserved for employees was subscribed over two times while the part reserved for RIL shareholders was subscribed a little over four times.
In the unofficial market, speculators are betting that the company will be listing at about Rs 1,360, a mark-up (also called the grey market premium or GMP) of Rs 241 over the upper limit of the IPO price band. The current GMP is slightly lower than Rs 273, the highest level seen a day before the IPO opened, but much higher than the opening quote of Rs 148 on Oct 4, quotes from websites tracking the trend in the unofficial market for shares showed. The strong response to the IPO comes on the back of a Rs 2.5 lakh-crore anchor book that was subscribed 30 times the size, which was Rs 8,110 crore, disclosures showed.

briefs.headline: Videos, the new gateway reshaping online retail
briefs.deck: Social media platforms such as Instagram and YouTube had already made access easier than ever—people sat at their homes, browsed through videos, subscribing to influencer-led recommendations and buying products. Platforms took note of the shopping habit and launched their own video and live formats. Amazon, for instance, launched Live in 2022 while players such as Myntra and Meesho joined in…
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Indians are no longer just shopping; they are video-shopping. Videos drive a lot of traction on online platforms such as Amazon, Flipkart, Myntra and Meesho. Consumers scroll through creator-led content reels or shorts, discovering a host of new brands and products with many eventually clicking on the ‘buy’ tab, often embedded in them. The trend is more popular among Gen Z shoppers and consumers residing in smaller towns, companies said.
For one, there’s live commerce wherein creators showcase a product or give demonstrations in real time. The other format is shortform shoppable videos which may or may not always feature creators and may not be live, but they allow people to buy products without leaving the video stream by way of links included within them. Live commerce and shoppable videos have both scaled to collectively create a content-to-commerce ecosystem. For Bengaluru-based IT professional Sanjeet Singh, influencer reels play a big role in product discovery. “Reels give me an idea of what the product is,” Singh said.
For one, there’s live commerce wherein creators showcase a product or give demonstrations in real time.
Social media platforms such as Instagram and YouTube had already made access easier than ever—people sat at their homes, browsed through videos, subscribing to influencer-led recommendations and buying products. 
Platforms took note of the shopping habit and launched their own video and live formats.
Amazon, for instance, launched Live in 2022 while players such as Myntra and Meesho joined in after a couple of years or so. The strategy seemed to have worked—creator-led discovery has influenced the shopping journeys of nearly two crore consumers on Amazon so far in 2026 while for Meesho, active order-generating content grew by over 140% to 1.7 million in Q1FY27, the firms said.
Besides, all the e-commerce companies have active accounts on platforms such as Instagram wherein they collaborate with influencers to market their products and sale events, amplifying visibility.
Creator-led commerce will become a key driver for e-commerce growth, contributing nearly $25 billion in gross merchandise value (GMV) by 2030, a joint April study by Deloitte and Google showed. “Creator content will scale significantly, with creator-owned storefronts and online videos becoming instantly shoppable. Eventually, these formats will also help onboard 50-60 million new online shoppers from tier 2 markets by effectively addressing key barriers around trust, product understanding, and quality,” analysts said in the report.
Cos’ video strategy
Amazon has scaled Live beyond real-time product demonstrations and creator recommendations to shortform, shoppable video experiences that are integrated directly into the shopping journey. “Short-form shopping videos complement live commerce and help keep product discovery contextual and engaging. The video format helps customers understand how a product works, see it in a real-life context, compare options, ask questions and move directly towards purchase,” said Nidhi Thakkar, head of social commerce, emerging countries at Amazon.
Nearly 70% of creator-led purchases on Amazon marketplace have come from non-metro cities, including cities such as Bathinda, Bhubaneswar, Coimbatore and Dehradun. “This reflects the role regional creators are playing in helping customers discover products through content that is relevant to their language, context and communities,” Thakkar added.
Myntra launched Ultimate Glam Clan (UGC) in Aug 2024—a shopper creator programme which enables customers to create fashion and beauty content around products they discover and shop on the platform. UGC grew to more than eight million sign-ups and 12 million cumulative pieces of content as of Sept 2026, the company claimed.
It also built Glamstream in July 2025, which brings together creator-led video, entertainment and commerce within the Myntra app. “Video is increasingly becoming an important part of the discovery journey, helping consumers explore fashion and beauty through creator recommendations, styling inspiration and realworld context. Users engaging with social commerce content convert around 10% better than those who do not, highlighting the role of content in influencing purchase decisions,” said Deepash Jain, vice-president, marketing, Myntra, adding that the format has enabled platforms to move beyond traditional catalogue-led shopping.
Flipkart’s video commerce ecosystem spans shortform videos, live shopping, creator-led product demos, Q&As, gamified formats and seamless in-video shopping journeys. “Shopping in India is increasingly being shaped by what consumers watch, share and trust,” said Ramesh Gururaja, senior vice president, consumer products and growth, FCC, Ads and Cleartrip at Flipkart.

briefs.headline: The real crisis in India’s fisheries
briefs.deck: Official claims that most of India’s marine fish stocks are sustainable should not distract from the continuing degradation of the country’s inshore fishing grounds; stronger governance of coastal waters and better management of mechanised trawling are essential for truly sustainable fisheries
briefs.bodyText:
India has a very large and old marine fishing population. Every day, both small-scale and mechanised trawl fishers go out to earn a living and provide the nation with food.
The Government of India recently released its latest prognosis of the country’s ocean fisheries (February 11, 2026). Its press release emphasised that Indian marine fisheries are largely sustainable, suggesting the country has avoided the bane of international fishing, namely overfishing.
Official claims
Drawing on figures compiled by the Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute (CMFRI), the government said that most commercial fish stocks “are in good health”. Furthermore, it stated that “91.1% of the 135 fish stocks evaluated in different regions during 2022 were found sustainable.” If this assessment is accurate, it would be good news. However, there are good reasons to doubt whether it is indeed correct.
For one, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) is far more reserved in its assessment of the condition of Indian marine fisheries than the Indian government seems to be. India’s country profile argues that “India’s marine fisheries production reached a plateau as most major stocks are fully exploited. […] Unregulated access to these fisheries resulted in significant overcapacity, especially of medium and small trawlers that compete over dwindling fishery resources with mostly impoverished small-scale fishers.” This message is not half as buoyant as the one published by the Indian government.
I will not dispute CMFRI’s conclusions or its methodology for calculating ‘sustainability’. After all, most of its procedures are veiled in secrecy. What is known, however, is that compared with many other fishing nations, CMFRI continues to rely primarily on landing data rather than stock assessments.
In other words, it calculates the availability of fish stocks in India’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) — which includes up to 200 nautical miles (371 km) of sea area around the country — based on what fishermen catch. Even a layperson can understand that finding a certain number of shells on the beach does not necessarily predict the quantity of shells in the sea.
Other nations, therefore, make use of stock assessments at sea itself, thereby calculating how much aquatic life is available in certain waters. This is obviously the more reliable method to determine the health of fish stocks.
The Government of India cannot be blamed for not yet adopting this more costly form of stock assessment. But it does raise suspicions that the race to catch up with China, which is also infecting the fisheries sector, may also be inducing a hidden bias in the figures.
The decline of inshore ecosystems
Among the fishers I have spoken to over thirty years along the Tamil Nadu coast, the consensus is that catches have consistently gone down and that many species that were formerly available have disappeared. The government, however, seems to continue on the path of amplifying fish production figures from one year to the next.
Overfishing, however, is not the central issue here. The more pressing concern is the decline, if not the destruction, of the inshore benthic environment. Over the past year, numerous fisheries scientists and policymakers have described the inshore fishing environment as “destroyed”. What exactly do they mean?
India is surrounded by a relatively narrow continental shelf, where fishing is always the most productive. This continental shelf is broadest in Gujarat and a part of Maharashtra, but remains quite narrow along the rest of the sub-continent.
Generally speaking, one can assume that the territorial seas — a legal category referring to waters that lie within 12 nautical miles (or 22 km) from shore — largely overlap with the continental shelf. These waters provide favourable ecological conditions for commercially valuable species such as shrimp to feed, breed and grow.
But why do senior experts conclude this is no longer the case?
This is a complex question with many answers. Thus, one can point to the construction of dams in major rivers, which disallow land-based nutrients from entering the sea. One can also point to the ongoing destruction of mangroves, where fish breed, and to pollution that is entering the sea from various industrial, agricultural, and urbanising sources. Many scientists, and fishers too, point to such changes to explain the decline of fisheries. These factors obviously affect the inshore fishing zone more than they do distant waters.
Mechanised trawling and its cost
One of the many factors contributing to this decline is the dramatic and largely uncontrolled expansion of mechanised trawling.
It is good to remind ourselves first of all that semi-industrial trawling is not an Indian fishing method. It was introduced from abroad around 1960 and has since expanded to gigantic proportions.
According to the same government press release, India now has 64,414 mechanised fishing vessels. These numbers are growing day by day as there are practically no restrictions on new entries. Moreover, existing vessels are continuously being extended and fitted with more powerful Chinese engines, enabling them to catch even more fish.
This oversized fleet of mechanised trawlers ploughs the inshore seabed in a continuous fashion. In heavily trawled areas, this results in a decline of all animal and plant life. It has also resulted in major conflicts with the numerous population of small-scale fishers who see their livelihoods imperilled. The problem is that regulations to protect the inshore fishing zone are almost non-existent. Yes, mechanised boat fishing is closed for two months every year, so as to allow for the rejuvenation of fish stocks. But the main tool to prevent unwanted trawling — the prohibition for mechanised boat fishers to operate within a geographic zone of 5 NM — lacks forcefulness.
There are two main reasons for this. First, coastal States lack sufficient staff or craft to patrol the inshore waters. Second, governments have precluded fishers from playing a helpful role in management. The result is that the ecology of the inshore fishing zone is continuously being degraded, and all fishers — small-scale and mechanised — are being pushed out to the offshore and the deep-sea fishing zones.
Rethinking fisheries policy
The Indian government is optimistic about the potential of deep-sea fishing and is encouraging fishers to make a shift. But the question is whether that potential, which is also being tapped by other fishing nations, is as bountiful as expected. The FAO estimates that “at best, only a marginal increase can be realised through exploitation of deep-sea resources.”
More fundamentally, India’s current fisheries policy is wasting the enormous potential of inshore waters. For one thing, it imposes extra expenses for fuel and technology on fishers so that they can actually travel to more distant waters. At the same time, it is closing its eyes to the dire need for proper management of inshore waters. Aside from addressing the problems of marine pollution, it also means curbing, if not reducing, mechanised boat fishing. This is more than a technical issue. Mechanised boat fishers, by way of their numbers and their political influence, now often stand in the way of proper management. This is witnessed, for example, in the case of the Palk Bay, which is located between India and Sri Lanka. There, the Indian fleet of mechanised boat fishers now pirates Sri Lankan waters to the detriment of small-scale fishers on the other side of the international border. Ownership of the island Katchatheevu does not make any difference in this respect.
The way forward
While the government’s assessment paints an encouraging picture of Indian fish stocks, a more fundamental concern remains. The larger issue is that fishers, scientists and policymakers continue to decry the degradation of the inshore fishing grounds. A viable and truly sustainable fishery can only be realised if governance of the so productive inshore waters improves. For this, the government must adjust its perspective. This is in line with FAO’s view that: “Strenuous efforts are needed at federal and state levels to upgrade the country’s capacity to manage its marine fisheries.” In this context, CMFRI might also want to devote effort to studying what the condition of the benthic environment is actually like. This would provide a basis for deliberating on the best way forward.
(Maarten Bavinck is emeritus professor of coastal resource governance, University of Amsterdam, email: j.m.bavinck@uva.nl)

briefs.headline: Why managing fiscal is a tightrope for State governments
briefs.deck: Most State government expenditure is on social sectors, such as health and education, and economic sectors, such as agriculture and irrigation. In Kerala, such spending has driven social progress since the 1960s. The gap between expenditure and receipts is usually financed through market borrowings.
briefs.bodyText:
Kerala and Tamil Nadu are among the most socially and economically advanced States in India. Yet, the finances of both governments, like those of most other States, are under stress. The White Papers recently released by the two governments described their outstanding debt as alarming. State government debt is often vilified as the result of fiscal mismanagement. But it may, in fact, reflect a mismatch between development aspirations and the limited fiscal capacity of State governments.
Debts build up over the years with deficits, which arise when the government’s expenditure overshoots its tax and other receipts. In India, while the power to raise taxes rests largely with the Union government, a larger share of overall government spending is borne by the State governments. A majority of the State government expenditure is on social sectors, such as health and education, and economic sectors, such as agriculture and irrigation, all of which have a direct impact on people’s lives and livelihoods. In Kerala, the high levels of State government spending on social sectors since the 1960s have been a central constituent of the public action driving social progress. Compared with the corresponding average for all Indian States, per capita State government social expenditure was higher in Kerala and Tamil Nadu (by 30% and 20%, respectively). In contrast, it was markedly lower in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh (by 35% and 40%) (for the period 2020-23, according to an analysis based on State Finances: A Study of Budgets, Reserve Bank of India).

briefs.bodyText:
Chennai Petroleum Corporation Ltd (CPCL) reported a net profit of ₹2,271 crore for the second quarter of FY2026-27, more than three times the ₹732 crore recorded in the corresponding quarter last year, as its gross refining margin improved sharply.
Revenue from operations rose to ₹22,109 crore in the quarter ended September 30, from ₹20,069 crore a year earlier. Profit before tax increased to ₹3,032 crore from ₹994 crore, according to the company’s financial performance statement dated October 22.
CPCL’s gross refining margin (GRM) rose to $20.41 per barrel in the September quarter, compared with $9.04 per barrel in the year-earlier period.
The company processed 2.590 million metric tonnes (MMT) of crude oil during the quarter, achieving a capacity utilisation of 98%, despite planned turnaround maintenance of one of its crude units.
For the six months ended September 30, CPCL’s revenue from operations increased to ₹51,486 crore from ₹38,762 crore in the corresponding period last year. Net profit rose to ₹3,288 crore from ₹675 crore.

stories.bodyText:

stories.headline: USA to host women's football Club World Cup in 2028 - FIFA
stories.deck: The U.S. has a proven track record of staging large sporting events, notably co-hosting the men's World Cup earlier this year
stories.bodyText:
The United States will host the inaugural women's football Club World Cup in 2028, FIFA announced on Thursday (October 22, 2026).
"The decision was taken in view of its experience in organising FIFA tournaments, the maturity of its infrastructure and services and the level of stakeholder interest in women's football in the country," world football's governing body said.
The U.S. has a proven track record of staging large sporting events, notably co-hosting the men's World Cup earlier this year.
The first-ever women's Club World Cup will be staged from January 5-30, 2028.
It will bring together 19 top-tier clubs from all six continental confederations.
The AFC (Asia), CAF (Africa), CONCACAF (North America) and CONMEBOL (South America) will be represented by three clubs apiece at the competition, one team will fly the flag for the OFC (Oceania) and six of Europe's best sides will represent UEFA.
Seven clubs have already secured their berths at the tournament: Arsenal (England), Club America Femenil (Mexico), Barcelona (Spain), Gotham (United States), Naegohyang (North Korea), Corinthians (Brazil) and Wuhan Jiangda (China).
"These seven clubs, and a dozen more, will come together to show the strength and depth of women's club football to a global audience," said FIFA chief women's football officer Sarai Bareman.
"They will have the opportunity to tell their story, expand their fan base and represent their club on the world stage. They have thoroughly earned this opportunity to be part of history in the United States."
FIFA said the introduction of the tournament marked "a major milestone for the professionalisation and global expansion of the women's club game, giving elite club sides a true world stage to compete on every four years".
Initially slated for 2026, FIFA pushed the inaugural tournament back by two years so it enjoys a clear window following the 2027 women's World Cup and ahead of the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles.

stories.headline: Brook breaks Gill's fastest 200 record as Lanka pull off historic ODI run chase
stories.deck: England captain Harry Brook smashed a record-breaking 202 off 116 balls, becoming the first Englishman to score an ODI double-century and the fastest to reach 200. However, Sri Lanka chased down 430 to win by two wickets with one ball remaining. Pavan Rathnayake scored 130, while England suffered their second consecutive defeat, leaving their hopes of reaching the Lahore final in danger.
stories.bodyText:
England captain Harry Brook made history by scoring the fastest double-century in One-Day International (ODI) cricket, but his record-breaking innings could not prevent Sri Lanka from securing a thrilling two-wicket victory in their tri-series match on Thursday. Sri Lanka chased down a target of 430 with one ball remaining, leaving England at the bottom of the standings after two defeats.
Brook reached his double-century in just 114 balls, breaking the previous record of 117 deliveries held by India's Shubman Gill. The 27-year-old also became the first English batter to score an ODI double-century, surpassing Ben Stokes' previous national record of 182 runs.
He smashed 202 runs off 116 balls, hitting 21 fours and 10 sixes before being caught by Sahan Arachchige off Janith Liyanage on the final ball of England's innings. Joe Root also contributed with 69 runs off 66 balls as England posted a massive 429-4.
Brook, however, was disappointed that his historic achievement ended in defeat.
"Unfortunately, it (the record) doesn't matter now. I thought we were going to be in a good position but, unfortunately, it doesn't even count," Brook said.
"Heart-breaking. I think you've hit the nail on the head there. It's very disappointing that we haven't been able to defend 430, but that's life, that's cricket," he added.
Sri Lanka pull off historic run chase
Sri Lanka produced a remarkable batting display to complete the second-highest successful run chase in ODI history. Pavan Rathnayake led the charge with 130 off 106 balls, while Avishka Fernando and Dasun Shanaka both missed their centuries by just three runs.
Sri Lanka needed six runs from the final two balls when Liyanage hit Josh Tongue for a six over long-off to seal victory with one delivery remaining. Tongue finished as England's leading wicket-taker with 3-79.
Brook praised Sri Lanka's performance and admitted England failed to execute their bowling plans.
"You don't see many teams chase down 430 and hats off to Sri Lanka. They've played exceptionally well. We couldn't execute our skills enough with the ball and, again, they've just played an absolute blinder there ..."
England, who lost to Pakistan by 87 runs on Tuesday, now need to win their remaining two matches to keep their hopes of reaching the final in Lahore alive.
"We'll have a good chat about it now and over the next couple of days. We've got a good opportunity in the next couple of games to really try and get to that final in Lahore."

stories.headline: Bihar to host India-New Zealand Under-20 Rugby Series
stories.deck: Men’s and women’s teams from both countries arrive in Patna. Seven players from Bihar were selected for the Indian teams. Matches to be held at Rajgir Sports Complex in Nalanda
stories.bodyText:
Bihar is set to host an international sporting event to mark 100 years of sporting ties between India and New Zealand.
As part of the “100 Years of Unity Through Sport” initiative, the India-New Zealand Under-20 Rugby Series will be held at the Rajgir Sports Complex from October 23 to 28. in Nalanda.
The main matches of the series will take place on October 27. The event will bring together young players from both countries to promote cultural exchange and mutual cooperation alongside sporting competition.
The Under-20 men’s and women’s teams from India and New Zealand have arrived in Bihar to participate in the series. The New Zealand teams received a traditional welcome at Patna airport on Thursday (October 22, 2026).
During their stay, players from both countries will participate in joint training sessions and share their sporting techniques, experiences and cultures.
New Zealand’s Under-20 Rugby teams have travelled to India for the first time for an event of this kind. New Zealand’s men’s team, Tama Toa, and women’s team, Hine Toa, comprise a total of 24 young Maori players selected from different regions.
The event will provide young athletes with an opportunity to showcase their talent on an international platform apart from strengthening the historic sporting ties between the two countries.
The selection of seven players from Bihar for the Indian Under-20 men’s and women’s teams is a matter of pride for the state. Bajrangi Kumar and Rohit Kumar have been included in the men’s team, while Alpana Kumari, Aarti Kumari, Beauty Kumari and Saloni Kumari have secured places in the women’s team. Sagar Prakash is also part of the Indian contingent.
Sagar Prakash, Alpana Kumari and Aarti Kumari previously represented India at the Asia Rugby Emirates Under-20 Sevens Championship held in Bihar in 2025.
According to official of Bihar Sports Deparmtent, four rugby sevens matches will be played at the Rajgir Sports Complex on October 27. These will include matches between the men’s teams and the women’s teams of India and New Zealand, along with two mixed matches.
The official asserted that players from both countries will come together to form joint teams for the mixed matches. The initiative aims to promote not only competition but also sportsmanship, cooperation and international friendship, the official said.
Rajgir is strengthening its reputation as a major destination for Rugby tournaments. The city hosted the Asia Rugby Emirates Under-20 Championship in August 2025 and the Senior National Rugby Championship in April 2026.
Hosting India-New Zealand series will further highlight Bihar’s sporting infrastructure and its capacity to organise international competitions.
Bihar State Sports Authority Director General-cum-CEO Raveendran Sankaran said hosting the series was a proud occasion for Bihar and Rajgir. He noted that the event would strengthen international sporting relations, encourage cultural exchange and inspire young people in the state to take up Rugby.
He added that the state government was committed to providing athletes with better training facilities and more opportunities to compete.
Indian Rugby Football Union President Rahul Bose said the completion of 100 years of sporting ties between India and New Zealand was a historic milestone. Playing against New Zealand on home soil would give Indian players an opportunity to learn international techniques and improve their understanding of the game.
Meanwhile, Manu Albert, head of the New Zealand Rugby delegation, expressed enthusiasm about sharing sporting experiences, developing the sevens format and supporting the training of Indian players and coaches.
Training workshops were organised at Kalinga stadium in Bhubaneswar for 35 Indian coaches, with support from New Zealand Rugby coaches in May 2026. The upcoming series in Rajgir represents an important step towards taking this collaboration forward.

briefs.headline: Asian Para Games: Thulasimathi clinches silver, remains in contention for two more golds
briefs.deck: Thulasimathi Murugesan showcased her talent by winning a silver medal in the women's singles SU5 badminton finals at the Asian Para Games. Despite putting up a strong fight, she fell short to Yang Qiuxia from China, with final scores of 18-21 and 11-21. This comes after her impressive semi-final comeback against World No. 1 Manisha Ramdass.
briefs.bodyText:
India's 
Thulasimathi Murugesan
 added another medal to her growing collection at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games, settling for silver in the women's singles SU5 badminton event after losing to China's Yang Qiuxia in the final on Friday. The 24-year-old, who won silver at the Paris 2024 Paralympics, went down 18-21, 11-21 against the Chinese shuttler at the Ichinomiya City Municipal Gymnasium.
However, Thulasimathi's campaign is far from over, with the Indian still in contention for two more gold medals in the mixed doubles and women's doubles events. She will look to make amends in the remaining finals as India aim to add to their medal tally.
Thulasimathi falls short against Yang after impressive semi-final comeback
Thulasimathi, currently ranked World No. 2, could not overcome Yang in the title clash, with the Chinese player securing the gold medal in straight games. The Indian had produced a fighting performance in the semi-finals, rallying from a game down to defeat compatriot and World No. 1 Manisha Ramdass 19-21, 21-15, 21-13 and book her place in the final.
The silver medal adds to Thulasimathi's impressive record in para-badminton, following her breakthrough performance at the Paris 2024 Paralympics, where she finished runner-up in the women's singles SU5 category.
Two more gold medal opportunities await
Thulasimathi will have two more chances to finish her campaign on a high. 
She has partnered Nitesh Kumar to reach the mixed doubles SL3-SU5 final, where the Indian duo will face Indonesia's Leani Ratri Oktila and Hikmat Ramdani.
The Indians booked their place in the final after overcoming China's Li Mingpan and Xiao Zuxian in a hard-fought 42-minute semi-final. Nitesh and Thulasimathi prevailed 21-19, 14-21, 21-17 to secure their place in the gold medal match.
Later, Thulasimathi will team up with Manasi Girishchandra Joshi in the women's doubles SL3-SU5 final. The Indian pair will face China's Yang Qiuxia and Xiao Zuxian, giving Thulasimathi another opportunity to challenge for gold against the Chinese shuttler who defeated her in the singles final.
Who is Thulasimathi Murugesan?
Born on April 11, 2002, in Kancheepuram, Tamil Nadu, Thulasimathi has established herself as one of India's leading para-badminton players. Her silver medal at the Paris 2024 Paralympics marked a major milestone in her career, while her performances at the Asian Para Games have further strengthened her standing on the international stage.
She trains in Hyderabad under coaches Pullela Gopichand and Irfan Sait while pursuing a degree in veterinary science at Namakkal. In recognition of her achievements in para-badminton, including her Paralympic success, she was also honoured with the Arjuna Award.

India's tally swelled to 88 at the Asian Para Games on Thursday. Sheetal, the 19-year-old sensation who is the reigning world champion and also the world number one, first combined with Toman Kumar to defend the mixed team gold against Indonesia's Teodora Audi Ayudia Ferelly and Ken Swagumilang 151-148.
She then overcame a four-point deficit to defeat Singapore's Alim Nur Syahidah 142-139 in a repeat of the Hangzhou 2023 individual final.
The day started perfectly for India with Suvarna Raj taking the gold medal in women's F54 discus throw with a best effort of 15.66m. The wheelchair-bound 44-year-old delivered a consistent performance, recording four throws beyond the 15-metre to secure the biggest win of her career.
It got progressively better for the country, which now has 88 medals in its kitty, including 21 gold, 26 silver and 41 bronze as medals also came in from para-swimming, para-badminton and para-table tennis.

Among the standout performances of the day was a Shailesh Kumar-led sweep of the men's high jump T63 event, and gold medals from sprinters Anjanaben Bumbadiya and Dilip Mahadu Gavit in their respective 400m T47 competitions.
Teenage Indian para swimmer Ravi Budigina won his third medal at the Asian Para Games 2026, claiming bronze in the men's 50m freestyle S13 event in Nagoya on Thursday. Kapil Kumar and Swatik Patil also finished on the podium in their respective events, taking India's medal tally in swimming to nine.
The 18-year-old visually impaired swimmer from Andhra Pradesh clocked 25.89 seconds to finish third in the 50m freestyle. He had earlier won silver medals in the men's S13 100m backstroke and 100m freestyle events.
Para archer Sheetal Devi picked up two gold medals in the space of less than two hours to reaffirm her peerless credentials, while the track-and-field contingent remained the single biggest contributor to India's tally that swelled to 88 at the Asian Para Games on Thursday.

briefs.headline: Sri Lanka trumps Brook's fastest double century to beat England by two wickets in cricket tri-series
briefs.deck: Brook's 116-ball 202 propelled England to its fourth highest ODI score of 429-4 before it ran into Sri Lanka's super counterpunch to lose by two wickets
briefs.bodyText:
Sri Lanka trumped Harry Brook's fastest-ever double century with the second-highest successful run chase in ODI history and handed England a second successive defeat in the tri-series on Thursday (October 23, 2026).
Brook's 116-ball 202 propelled England to its fourth highest ODI score of 429-4 before it ran into Sri Lanka's super counterpunch to lose by two wickets.
Needing six runs off Josh Tongue's final two balls, Janith Liyanage lofted the fast bowler over long-off for a winning six to reach 430-8 and earn Sri Lanka their most memorable ODI victory since winning the 1996 World Cup.
Sri Lanka's astonishing run-chase was only second behind South Africa's 438-9 when it beat Australia by one wicket at Johannesburg in 2006.
"Incredible game of cricket, both teams were exceptional," Brook said. "Sri Lanka just outplayed us. They played exceptional cricket to knock off 400."
Rathnayake, Shanaka and Fernando star
Avishka Fernando, recalled for the tri-series since last playing an ODI in January 2025, and Pavan Rathnayake set up the strong chase with a 166-run third-wicket stand after Sri Lanka lost two wickets inside the first five overs of the run chase.
Fernando missed out on a century but his 97-run knock off 83 balls kept Sri Lanka well in the game. Dasun Shanaka, also returning to the ODI fold after more than two years, then added another electrifying 133 runs with Rathnayake off just 79 balls as the England bowlers had no answer to the belligerence of Sri Lanka's batters on a batting wicket.
Rathnayake completed his second ODI century and made 130 off 106 balls with 15 fours and three sixes as he brought down the target to 107 runs off the final 58 balls before holing out to long-on.
But Shanaka, who twice successfully overturned decisions against him through television reviews, continued toying with England's fast bowlers and smashed eight sixes and six boundaries with Sam Curran returning expensive figures of 2-103.
England sneaked back in the 44th over when Shanaka missed out on a deserved century and was caught at long-on and left Sri Lanka needing 67 off the final six overs.
Dunith Liyanage then smashed three sixes and seven fours and scored a brisk unbeaten 61 off 27 balls as England kept on conceding boundaries.
With eight needed of the final over, Tongue uprooted the middle stumps of Wellalage and Eshan Malinga off successive balls but Asitha Fernando denied the fast bowler a hat trick and gave the strike back to Liyanage to finish off the game with a big hit.
"We chased very well today, I enjoyed it as captain," said Sri Lanka skipper Kusal Mendis, who was run out for duck at the non-striker's end without facing a ball. "Me and coach spoke to the batters and said to play the first couple of overs normally … everyone believed we can do it."
Brook's double century
Brook needed 114 balls for the double ton and holed out two balls later for 202 off the final ball of England's innings after captain Kusal Mendis won his fifth successive toss on the tour of Pakistan and elected to field.
Brook reached his first century off 75 balls with a ramped boundary over fine leg. He then reached 150 with a similar shot, and took 39 balls to hit the second century, reached with a paddle sweep against Janith Liyanage in the final over.
"It was a nice innings but being on the losing side it has no value whatsoever in my eyes," Brook said. "We got to get back to the drawing board a little bit, and we have an opportunity in the next couple of games to nail down a place in the final."
Brook's effort was two balls less than Shubman Gill's record of 116 balls which the Indian made against West Indies at Guwahati last month.
Joe Root (69), Will Jacks (66 not out) and Tom Banton (50) also contributed to England's monster total after being sent in.
Sri Lanka fast bowlers Malinga (0-91) and Dilshan Madushanka (0-89) were blazed all around Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium while Shanaka was smacked for 74 off his six overs.
Left-arm spinner Wellalage returned with somewhat respectable figures of 2-56, but the seamers went for plenty as Brook and Jacks added a rapid 156 runs in the final 10 overs.
The tournament now moves to Lahore where England, which lost to Pakistan by 87 runs in the first match, takes on unbeaten Pakistan in the return game on Sunday

briefs.headline: Sindhu, Ashmita enter quarterfinals of French Open badminton
briefs.deck: Unseeded Ashmita was the star of the day, upsetting world No. 2 and third seed Yamaguchi 21-19 21-18 in a second-round match that lasted 37 minutes
briefs.bodyText:
Double Olympic medallist P.V. Sindhu and young Indian shuttler Ashmita Chaliha sailed into the women's singles quarterfinals with straight-game wins over Japan's Riko Gunji and Akane Yamaguchi, respectively, at the $950,000 French Open badminton tournament here on Thursday (October 22, 2026).
Unseeded Ashmita was the star of the day, upsetting world No. 2 and third seed Yamaguchi 21-19 21-18 in a second-round match that lasted 37 minutes.
Sindhu then prevailed over Gunji 21-12 21-16 in a match lasting 44 minutes to progress to the quarterfinals.
Earlier in the day, India's Ayush Shetty and Tanvi Sharma bowed out in the pre-quarterfinals of their respective events.
Taking the court first among the Indians, Tanvi was no match for world No. 1 and top seed An Se Young of South Korea, losing 11-21, 14-21 in a 37-minute women's singles match.
Later, Shetty forfeited his match against sixth seed Kodai Naraoka of Japan due to an undisclosed injury while trailing 17-21, 6-11 in a men's singles second-round match.
Shetty had earlier defeated compatriot Kidambi Srikanth in the opening round to progress in the tournament.

briefs.headline: Promising Indian sprinter Dondapati Jayaram dies in road accident
briefs.deck: Jayaram along with Malay Barik, another athlete, was going to Kataka for Dussehra celebration by bike on Wednesday evening when the accident occurred
briefs.bodyText:
In a tragic road accident, Dondapati Mrutyum Jayaram, a promising athlete who brought laurels to the country at the national and international levels, died in a road accident near Cuttack late on Wednesday (October 21, 2026) evening.
Jayaram, along with Malay Barik, another athlete, was travelling to Cuttack to celebrate Dussehra when they reportedly lost control of their motorcycle and crashed into a road median. Doctors at SCB Medical College and Hospital in Cuttack declared both of them brought dead.
Originally hailing from Kakinada, Andhra Pradesh, he lived in Bhabanipatna, Kalahandi district, Odisha. He trained at the Odisha Reliance Foundation Athletics High Performance Centre in Bhubaneswar under coaches Rohit Mane and Martin Owens.
A promising talent in the 100-metre and 200-metre sprints and the 4×100-metre relay, Jayaram has represented Odisha’s junior and senior teams and India’s Under-20 men’s team. The departed athlete won one silver and one bronze medal in the 4×100m relay and the 100m sprint, respectively, in the 4th South Asian Junior Athletics Championship, held at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium in Chennai from September 11–13, 2024.
Besides, he was part of the Indian men’s 4×100m relay team that won the bronze medal with a national record of 40.01 seconds in the 21st Asian Junior (U-20) Athletics Championships at the Dubai Police Stadium in Dubai on April 27, 2024.
Recently, he had won one silver and one bronze medal in men’s 200m and 100m run respectively at the 6th Indian Open U-23 athletics competition held Sawai Mansingh Stadium, Jaipur, October 16-18, 2026.
Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi condoled death athletes saying their untimely passing was a profound loss to Odisha’s sporting fraternity.

briefs.headline: Women in Blue start firm favourites as focus shifts to ODIs
briefs.deck: Jintimani replaces injured pacer Renuka; Zimbabwe will hope to pose a tough question or two to the World champion
briefs.bodyText:
There’s little that can dent the momentum of a high-flying Indian team at home, in its favourite format – One Day Internationals – hosting a side ranked 11 places below it: Zimbabwe. More so after a dominant 3-0 sweep of the T20I leg of a historic maiden bilateral engagement.
But one thing can: injuries. Fitness issues in India’s seam resources have been a thorn in the side of the reigning 50-over World champion, and its resistance faces a setback with Renuka Singh ruled out courtesy of not building the required bowling volume for 50-over cricket at the BCCI Centre of Excellence.
The Women’s Premier League and changes (however slow) in prioritising pace at the domestic level have pushed a greater raw pool to the doors of the team which means this type of an absence won’t sting as much as it would have a few years ago. But with the inaugural Women’s Champions Trophy around the corner, India will sweat over Renuka’s fitness and bowling rhythm.
The task for the present, however, is to replicate its T20I dominance over the Lady Chevrons in the one-day series too. And India’s bulging batting muscle perhaps has that job in the bag comfortably.
Jemimah Rodrigues’ absence due to injury means the door opens for someone like Yastika Bhatia and Tejal Hasabnis — who have registered stellar scores at the A level recently — or Harleen Deol, part of the World Cup-winning side in 2025 but who has since lost fallen out of favour.
Life is quiet in the village of Kotambi, where the Baroda Cricket Association Stadium, which will host this leg, is situated. It’s a quiet green lung off the state highway, but these two teams will hope to turn up the decibels.
Josephine Nkomo’s side is far from a pushover, and will hope to pose a tough question or two to the ODI behemoth.
The teams: India: Smriti Mandhana (Capt.), Deepti Sharma (Vice-capt.), Shafali Verma, Pratika Rawal, Harmanpreet Kaur, Harleen Deol, Tejal Hasabnis, Richa Ghosh (wk), Yastika Bhatia (wk), Vaishnavi Sharma, Nandani Sharma, Shree Charani, Kranti Gaud, Sayali Satghare, Jintimani Kalita.
Zimbabwe: Josephine Nkomo (Capt.), Kelis Ndhlovu, Beloved Biza, Chipo Mugeri-Tiripano, Chiedza Dhururu (wk), Nyasha Gwanzura, Modester Mupachikwa, Sharne Mayers, Loryn Phiri, Francisca Chipare, Kudzai Chigora, Nomvelo Sibanda, Olinder Chare, Michelle Mavunga, Tendai Makusha.
